title: Shania Twain says she's finally 'getting it right' in her 60s after starting life ‘on the tough side’
summary: Shania Twain opened up about how childhood poverty, stage fright and a Lyme disease battle shaped her journey to finding peace in her 60s.
story: Shania Twain told Fox News Digital at the 2024 Peoples Choice Country Awards that shes embracing the "evolution of country music."
Shania Twain is looking back on her long journey from an impoverished childhood in rural Canada to international superstardom and finally coming to terms with her past in her 60s.
During a recent interview with "CBS Mornings," the 60-year-old singer opened up about her difficult upbringing and how she has gained a new outlook later in life.
"I started life out a little bit on the tough side," Twain said. "In my 60s now, I feel like I've really gotten it, or I'm just now getting all of that right."
Shania Twain opened up about how she feels she is finally "getting it right" in her 60s. (Matthew Baker/Getty Images for ABA)
When asked by CBS correspondent Seth Doane about why her 60s had given her that perspective, Twain had a simple answer.
SHANIA TWAIN'S LIQUID DIET HELPS HER AVOID A ‘NIGHTMARE’ CONCERT MISHAP

"You know what it is? It's called time," she said. "I'd love to have been able to get it right in my 50s, but I just – that wasn't enough time. I needed to be in my 60s to start getting it right, you know?"

Born Eilleen Regina Edwards in Windsor, Ontario, Twain was raised in the small town of Timmins by her mother, Sharon, and adoptive father Jerry Twain after her biological parents divorced when she was 2 years old.
Twain spoke candidly about starting life "on the tough side." (Mathew Tsang/Getty Images)
TAYLOR HICKS CREDITS FAITH AND BLUE-COLLAR BIRMINGHAM ROOTS FOR KEEPING HIM GROUNDED AFTER 'AMERICAN IDOL' WIN
Twain's family struggled financially, and the singer has spoken candidly about growing up in poverty and witnessing domestic abuse at home.
While speaking with "CBS Mornings," Twain recalled that she was forced to grow up quickly, taking on burdens that far exceeded those of a typical child.

"When I was younger, I was so over-responsible for the household," she remembered. "My mother was depressed a lot of the time. She spent a lot of her days in bed. She lived off coffee and cigarettes that I would bring her in bed just to see if she was still alive."
VANILLA ICE SAYS HE NEARLY JOINED THE ‘27 CLUB’ BEFORE QUITTING DRUGS FOR GOOD
"There was a lot of violence in the house," Twain added. "And we didn't eat well a lot of the times. We weren't clothed properly a lot of the time."
The singer began performing at bars when she was just 8 to help support her family. (Robert Smith/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)
Long before becoming one of country music's biggest stars, Twain performed in bars as a child to help support her family, including her mother, stepfather and four siblings.
The singer shared that her early performing years led her to develop stage fright, which would plague her for most of her career regardless of her audience size.

"The amount of people is not necessarily what affected me over the years with stage fright," Twain said. "It was starting so young in bars that were, you know, I was 8 years old, and the bars were smoky, and everyone was intoxicated. I don't know what I'm actually singing about, because I'm singing about divorce, and I'm eight."
Twain explained that she did not realize how deeply those experiences had shaped her until much later in life.

"This was just an uncomfortable place to be as a child, and I carried that with me," she said. "And only in my 50s, I finally just said, 'Whoa. I've got my voice. I have an audience. I have everything to just celebrate.' And the fear just dropped away."
Twain explained that her early years as a child performer led her to have stage fright for decades. (Jim Spellman/WireImage)

Twain's challenges did not end with her difficult childhood. In 1987, when she was 22, her mother and stepfather were killed in a car accident. While both Twain and her older sister Jill were already adults, their three younger siblings, including sister Carrie-Ann and brothers Mark and Darry, were underage and needed a legal guardian.

At the time, Twain was trying to establish herself as a singer-songwriter after moving to Toronto to pursue music. However, Twain put her career on hold and moved back to Ontario to care for her younger siblings.
During a 2023 appearance on "The Drew Barrymore Show," Twain recalled the difficulties that she faced after becoming her siblings' primary caregiver.
GOLDIE HAWN THINKS KIDS LACK 'GRIT' FROM TOO MUCH SCREEN TIME, NOT ENOUGH REAL-WORLD PROBLEM SOLVING

"That was a different type of parenting because now there was nobody to blame because now they’re gone," she said. "All of a sudden, I’m responsible for making decisions about my parents’ mortgage. I didn’t know they had a mortgage, I didn’t know what it was, I didn’t know anything about how they ran their business or debts or insurance. I had to learn overnight. My parents died — three days later I’m in lawyer’s offices and insurance company offices."
Twain told "CBS Mornings" that with the benefit of time, she is now able to look back on those experiences with gratitude instead of focusing solely on the hardship.
The singer became her three younger siblings' primary caregiver after their parents died in a car accident. (Getty Images)

"When I reflect back on those times, I'm reflecting on them from where I am now, which is a very good place," Twain said. "Like, I made it out of there. It's like, 'Whoa, I'm just celebrating all of that.' And what makes me feel so accomplished, is staying connected to where I came from. It's the contrast that makes it feel so good."

After her siblings were older and living independently, Twain finally turned her attention back to her own dreams. In 1991, she moved to Nashville and signed a recording deal with the legendary country music label Mercury Nashville.

Twain's breakthrough came in 1995 with the release of her Grammy-winning sophomore album, "The Woman in Me." Two years later, she skyrocketed to global fame with "Come On Over," the best-selling album by a female artist of all time.
JANE SEYMOUR, 75, SHARES HOW SHE APPROACHES AGING WITH VITALITY: 'BEST I CAN BE'
Over the course of her career, Twain has sold more than 100 million records worldwide, won five Grammy Awards and cemented her status as a country music icon.
However, Twain faced new obstacles even after reaching superstardom, including divorce and a battle with Lyme disease.
Twain also battled Lyme disease that affected her vocal cords and didn't release a new album for 15 years. (Dave J Hogan)

In 2003, she was diagnosed with Lyme disease, which affected her vocal cords and threatened her singing career. The ordeal contributed to a 15-year gap between studio albums before she returned with 2017's "Now," which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart.
In 2018, Twain underwent open-throat surgery and returned to touring. During her appearance on "CBS Mornings," she reflected on regaining her voice after her health struggles.

"Once I made a sound, it was just there," Twain recalled. "I feel lucky. I don't want to make it sound easy! It wasn't easy, it was a very long road, but I just feel very grateful and very lucky that I have it back."
"I have more, like, of a fry to my voice, you know, a little gravel," she continued. "I don't mind that. I've embraced it. It's now part of my sound."
Twain explained that she has adapted to the changes in her voice since resuming her career.
"I've taken a different approach to singing my older songs," she said. "In fact, I've found new placements in my voice that I enjoy, you know, that I didn't have before."

"I love to experiment. I think it's the same with any art form," Twain added. "You have to experiment a little bit to get just the right – whatever's satisfying you the most at that time, you know?"
Twain recently fulfilled a lifelong dream when she performed at Toronto's legendary venue Horseshoe Tavern. (Jeffrey Mayer/WireImage)
Twain recently fulfilled a longtime dream when she surprised fans with a performance at Toronto's legendary Horseshoe Tavern.

After taking the stage on Friday night, she told the crowd, "I grew up in Northern Ontario and the dream in my little bar bands at the time, all through my youth and my teens, even in my 20s, was to play the Horseshoe Tavern."
"But we weren’t recognized … we just weren’t established enough, so we never made the hire here," she continued. "So this is my first time in the Horseshoe Tavern."

"I guess I’ve finally made it after all these years," Twain added as the crowd cheered. "It was really a big deal to be able to play the Horseshoe Tavern. We all talked about that up North, ‘Oh, maybe someday we can play the Horseshoe Tavern.’ And now I’m playing here. I feel like it’s a very full-circle moment,"
Twain said her new album "Little Miss Twain" is inspired by her journey. (Getty Images)
"My home province, with all you beautiful people, in this historic bar. This is so historical. So it’s a privilege to be here, finally."
While speaking with "CBS Mornings," Twain explained how viewing her past struggles through a new lens had inspired her new album "Little Miss Twain."

"'Little Miss Twain' is me, now, looking back at my child's self and the journey that child went through, from starting out in those bars at 8 years old, right up to when I got my recording contract in Nashville," she said.

"That's fine," she said. "I plan to live to be 200 anyway!"

title: Brad Paisley says Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce threw 'one of the least pretentious weddings' ever
summary: Brad Paisley says Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce's July 3 wedding was "one of the least pretentious" he'd ever attended despite hosting about 1,000 celebrity guests.
story: Fox News political analyst Gianno Caldwell and pundit Tiffany Smiley dissect the reported wedding of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce on 'Fox News Saturday Night.'
Despite hosting roughly 1,000 guests, Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce kept their wedding refreshingly down-to-earth, according to one country music star.
Brad Paisley praised the couple's July 3 nuptials as refreshingly humble, calling the event of the decade "one of the least pretentious weddings" he'd ever attended.

"I took this personally when I got the invite, because in the invite, it said, ‘If you’re getting this, you mean a lot to us,’" Paisley told The Associated Press. "And it was really fun to watch the cat-and-mouse game of like, ‘We can tell you roughly where it’s gonna be. We’re not gonna say what building... And here’s the date, and if you’re in, we’ll tell you more.’ And I was like, I went to my wife, I said, ‘Want to go?’ She’s like, ‘Absolutely. We’ve gotta be there.’ So we did it. It was RSVP yes."
TAYLOR SWIFT AND TRAVIS KELCE'S WEDDING LEAKS SNOWBALL AS GUESTS REVEAL INSIDE DETAILS

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce celebrated their July 3 wedding with roughly 1,000 guests, but country star Brad Paisley said it was "one of the least pretentious weddings" he has ever attended. (Getty Images)
"Ironically, one of the least pretentious weddings I’ve ever seen, or ever will see," he added. "And so, yeah, it meant a lot to be... It was kind of a big thank you from her to invite us."
Sports Illustrated Swimsuit model Camille Kostek echoed Paisley's sentiment, recalling a phone-free reception where guests danced for hours alongside fellow celebrities.

"I think we didn't have phones, and there was no sense of time in there," Kostek explained to Fox News Digital while attending Sports Illustrated Beyond the Pitch on July 18 alongside top athletes, celebrities and tastemakers during the World Cup. "I think I was probably on the dance floor for five straight hours. Shoes came off. It was so much fun."

Kostek recalled sharing the dance floor with country star Chris Stapleton and spotting Oscar-winning actress Julia Roberts during what she described as a memorable night.
"I didn't dance next to Taylor, she was up on stage, and I was like dancing from afar with her," Kostek added.

Swift and Kelce married on July 3 in front of 1,000 guests at Madison Square Garden, a representative for the pop star told Fox News Digital. The two opted not to have a traditional wedding party, instead choosing to have Swift's brother as her "Man of Honor" and Kelce's brother as his "Best Man."
Screens display a message referencing singer Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce outside Madison Square Garden, the venue for their reported wedding celebrations on July 3. (Getty Images)

Workers hang up curtains inside Madison Square Garden before Taylor Swift's wedding to Travis Kelce. (REUTERS/Christian Monterrosa)

The couple prioritized privacy throughout the celebration, taking steps to keep the ceremony and reception out of the public eye. People reported guests were asked to place their phones in individual locked glass boxes upon arrival, with each person receiving a key to access their devices later.

title: 'Game of Thrones' star Lena Headey says outrage over infamous nude scene left her stunned
summary: Lena Headey reveals why she used a body double for Cersei's "Walk of Atonement" and reflects on the predatory power dynamics young actresses face.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
More than 10 years after one of television's most talked-about scenes, Lena Headey set the record straight about a decision that sparked backlash far beyond Westeros.
Headey pulled back the curtain on the backlash that erupted after Cersei Lannister's infamous "Walk of Atonement" in "Game of Thrones," revealing she still found the outrage baffling.

"I was really shocked by the anger, by this idea that I’d duped the audience," Headey told The Telegraph. "But by that point everyone knew [the cast], it was insane simply going anywhere, and I was with 3,000 extras."
'OFF CAMPUS' STAR ELLA BRIGHT ADDRESSES AGE CONCERNS OVER INTIMATE SCENES IN PROVOCATIVE SERIES
Lena Headey reflected on the backlash she received after using a body double for Cersei Lannister's infamous "Walk of Atonement" scene in "Game of Thrones." (C Flanigan/Getty Images)

She explained that while acting is "a joy," the scale of filming the scene would have made it impossible for her to fully inhabit the emotional performance if she had also been worrying about being naked in front of thousands of people.
"I wouldn’t have been able to do the emotional part of the job," she told the outlet. "I’d have been in full-on defensive mode."

Looking back, Headey said she was in a very different position than many younger actresses entering the industry. Her experience on set gave her the confidence to set boundaries she doesn't believe everyone feels comfortable asserting.
GOLDIE HAWN SOUNDS THE ALARM ON CHILDHOOD CELEBRITY CULTURE: 'ALL I CAN SAY IS IT'S A NIGHTMARE'
Lena Headey and Nikolaj Coster-Waldau in a scene from season 7 of "Game of Thrones." The two played Cersei and Jaime Lannister in the series.  (Hbo/Kobal / Shutterstock)

"By that point, I’d been through the wringer," the actress said. "I could stand up for myself. I’m not saying those actresses couldn’t, but they were much younger and more vulnerable, and had far less experience of being in front of people and the camera and performing. Whereas I was of an age where I’d just tit about and diffuse anything uncomfortable with idiocy."
At the time, Headey told Entertainment Weekly some viewers believed she was "less of an actress" because she didn't perform the nudity herself.

"I've done nudity. I'm not averse to it," she explained in 2016. "But I know I'm a very emotional actor and I get really driven by that. In order to do my job, I allow myself to be really vulnerable. I don't know any other way to do my job. Things really affect me. And the thought of being naked for three days and trying to contain her in the way she would be I think I would feel very angry. I didn't want to be angry. I don't think Cersei would be angry. I did what I thought she would do, emotionally."
Lena Headey said filming Cersei Lannister's iconic "Game of Thrones" scene with thousands of extras made using a body double the right choice for her performance. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

Headey praised body double Rebecca Van Cleave for taking on the physically demanding role, acknowledging that appearing nude on camera was far from easy. She also said being a mother and an established public figure made filming the nude portions herself feel like more than she was willing to take on.
"I didn't phone it in," she noted of her performance. "I was actually there for three days with Rebecca."

Lena Headey portrayed the ruthless and power-hungry Queen Cersei Lannister throughout HBO's hit fantasy series "Game of Thrones," earning multiple Emmy nominations for the role. (Jason LaVeris/FilmMagic)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
For Headey, the controversy also reflected a much bigger issue she believes many actresses faced early in their careers.

"There was this rite of passage all young female actors had to go through, which usually involved snogging and falling in love, and having sex and showing your boobs," she told The Telegraph. "They’d call them the ingénue parts, to make it sound nicer."
The "300" actress admitted she rarely questioned those expectations when she was starting out because she was simply grateful to be working.

"But I just got on with it," she explained. "I didn’t go to drama school, so I would just arrive on a set and be, ‘Oh my God, I’ve got a job.’ And when it came to those moments, I don’t think I even questioned that I should be safe. Instead, I’d go home and cry, or think, ‘Oh, that felt weird and too familiar.’ Now I look back and feel, ‘Hmm, that was rough.’"
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Lena Headey said her early experiences in Hollywood shaped the boundaries she later set as an established actress, reflecting on changing attitudes toward women in the entertainment industry. (Getty Images)
Those experiences ultimately changed the way Headey viewed power dynamics throughout the entertainment industry.

"The weird protection that we offer predatory men in the business because of the disproportionate power they wield, set against the need among vulnerable actresses to work to put food on the table to get the job – it makes me very angry. A job can be completely soured by one person who, for some reason, is allowed to get away with it."
She said the #MeToo movement exposed how widespread those experiences were and believes younger actresses today are far more willing to reject situations that make them uncomfortable.
"The attitude today is, ‘I’m not f---ing doing that,'" she emphasized.

title: Hayden Panettiere defends giving up custody of her daughter despite intense 'emotional pain'
summary: Hayden Panettiere reveals in her memoir why she gave full custody of daughter Kaya to Wladimir Klitschko while battling postpartum depression.
story: The "Sleepwalker" actress told Fox News Digital that she has learned to not be so hard on herself as she gets older in the industry.
Hayden Panettiere is opening up about what she calls the most painful decision she's ever made as a mother.

In her memoir, "This Is Me: A Reckoning," the "Nashville" alum opens up about why she gave full custody of her daughter, Kaya, to her ex-fiancé, Wladimir Klitschko. Panettiere reveals that her 11-year-old daughter has lived with her father since 2018.
"I just knew that if I wanted to... I knew how bad a place I was in," the actress told Fox News Digital. "I hid it from my daughter as much as I could."
HAYDEN PANETTIERE SAYS FILMING ‘NASHVILLE’ WAS LIKE LIVING THROUGH ADDICTION TWICE
Hayden Panettiere is opening up about the heartbreaking decision that led to daughter Kaya living with ex-fiancé Wladimir Klitschko since 2018. (Storm Santos)

"When I saw her in the environment over there (in Europe) and the support system that she had, I said to myself, 'If I fight, if I go to war about this, it's going to permanently damage my child. It's going to be incredibly public. She's got two very famous parents, and it's going to be ugly.'"

"I said, 'You know what? Let her grow up here,'" she said. "I will travel here as much as I can. I know she's safe. I know she's well taken care of — beyond well taken care of. She has an incredible life. And I also knew that there would be a day when she would come back to me."
"This Is Me: A Reckoning" by Hayden Panettiere is out now. (Grand Central Publishing)
"I tried to numb myself," the 36-year-old admitted. "It was very hard to wrap my mind around the pain, the emotional pain of that. But you keep putting one foot in front of the other somehow."
WATCH: HAYDEN PANETTIERE EXPLAINS THE MENTAL AND PHYSICAL CHALLENGES OF MAKING NEW THRILLER ‘SLEEPWALKER’
In the book, Panettiere wrote that not being under the same roof as Kaya has been "the most gut-wrenching experience of my life."

"... I grieve that I'm not the mother I thought I'd be and definitely not the mother I want to be (trust me, no one should ever have to raise a child on FaceTime), and although I miss Kaya so much, my heart aches, I know how blessed I am to be her mom."
Hayden Panettiere told Fox News Digital she hopes sharing her story will help mothers battling postpartum depression feel less alone. (Bernd Thissen/Picture Alliance via Getty Images)
Panettiere reflected on filming "Nashville" while navigating a difficult pregnancy, which was ultimately written into her character Juliette Barnes' storyline.
On the set of "Nashville," art imitated life for Hayden Panettiere in ways she never expected. (Mark Levine/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Panettiere's pregnancy was marked by a series of frightening health scares. She described how doctors spotted concerning abnormalities during prenatal scans and warned that Kaya might have microcephaly. The actress sought solace in Hawaii, a place she has long considered a refuge.
While she was there, Klitschko shared a Ukrainian tradition for good luck, urging her to kneel before a tree, hold onto it and "thank God for everything He has given you and pray for what you need."
Hayden Panettiere is seen here in Hawaii shortly before her daughter was born. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)

Weeks later, Panettiere endured a life-threatening delivery. During her C-section, doctors called a "code crimson" after her blood wouldn't clot and her uterus became infected. She underwent three hours of emergency surgery.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Hayden Panettiere is seen with her growing baby bump. She gave birth on Dec. 9, 2014. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)
"I almost passed away while having my daughter," Panettiere told Fox News Digital. "I had seven blood transfusions. I didn't know if I was going to make it."
During her recovery, Panettiere struggled to bond with her daughter.
Hayden Panettiere and Wladimir Klitschko met at a party for a mutual friend in 2008. (Courtesy of Hayden Panettiere)

"You hear these stories from your friends about their experiences, and they're so positive," she said. "They also tell you about 'the baby blues.' At first, I thought, 'I just have the baby blues.' But it just kept going and going, deeper and deeper, worse and worse. And the doctors wouldn't even diagnose me with anything. My way of trying to cope with it was drinking because of the anxiety and the inability to sleep."
In her new memoir, Hayden Panettiere detailed the struggles she endured with postpartum depression. (Storm Santos)

"You are just discontent and unhappy all the time," Panettiere said. "You just feel like it's really dark. It doesn't make rational sense. It's not logical. And yet, you're trying to make sense of it. But when it's going on for 10 months afterward, you're like, there's something seriously wrong."

In the memoir, Panettiere recalled enduring "long days of nothingness stretching before me" as anxiety took over, becoming "the hulking monster that sits in your chest and erases your confidence and motivation." Despite having "everything I've ever wanted," she remained deeply "unhappy."
Wladimir Klitschko and Hayden Panettiere attend the Giorgio Armani show during Milan Menswear Fashion Week Spring/Summer 2014 on June 25, 2013, in Milan, Italy. (Venturelli/WireImage)
She self-medicated with alcohol. The actress entered treatment for the first time when Kaya was 4 months old after realizing her drinking had spiraled out of control.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

When Kaya was 4 months old, Hayden Panettiere sought treatment and was diagnosed with postpartum depression. She says the medications she was prescribed left her feeling numb and disconnected. (Storm Santos)
"When you wake up in the morning and the first thing you're thinking about is having a drink, it's a problem," Panettiere said.

"I just knew that I had to get help, do it for myself. I knew I was no good in the condition that I was in. I did everything that I could, and I came out sober, but I was still struggling with postpartum. But I was the one who asked to go to treatment."
"I walked into rehab addicted to one substance, and I walked out, completely dependent on something else," Hayden Panettiere wrote in her memoir. (Martin Rose/Bongarts/Getty Images)
Panettiere said she reached a breaking point and realized she needed professional help after alcohol became her way of coping with persistent postpartum depression following childbirth.

"I talked to my daughter's father about it, and I was like, 'I need help, professional help. I need somebody to fix me because this depression for the rest of my... is it ever going to go away? Is this the new normal? Am I going to have to just understand that I'm going to always be depressed for the rest of my life?' So when I went to treatment, it was me going, 'I'm at my breaking point. I need intervention. I need professionals. I need somebody to guide me through this.'"
Hayden Panettiere began her first regular acting role at age 4 in "One Life to Live." (Ron Galella/Getty Images; Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images)

In the book, Panettiere wrote that in 2015, the anxiety "crept back in, then overtook me," buzzing "like a fluorescent light, keeping me reactive, on edge and full of dread." She became reliant on prescription medication to help her cope.

As Panettiere continued battling addiction and mental health challenges, her relationship with Klitschko unraveled. In 2018, he presented her with papers seeking full custody of Kaya, telling her, "I want full custody. I worry about Kaya when she's with you."

Panettiere defended herself, insisting their daughter was always surrounded by loving caregivers and that she had "never been drunk and alone with Kaya" while she was in her care. "I was mortified when I saw stories like 'Hayden Panettiere gave up her daughter,'" she said.

"I was heartbroken. It's not like I live for other people's opinions of me, but I'm also a human being. Everyone wants to be understood. "I felt like I made the right call," she reflected. "I've seen who she is and she's an incredible human being. Something must have gone right."

Panettiere wrote that she has an "incredibly strong" bond with Kaya.

"I travel a lot to Europe, and I spend a lot of time on FaceTime with her," she explained. "And Wlad and I have a good relationship. We made a promise to each other that we would never say a bad word about each other to our child. That was something that I grew up with. And we've stuck to that."

"She's 11 now, so time is flying," Panettiere said. "I feel like she's becoming more and more curious about me, my life and who I am. We're so similar. She is me. I understand her in a way that nobody else can."

"I feel connected to myself," she said. "I feel like I'm taking good care of myself, checking in with myself. And I have a laundry list of things I would love to accomplish and create. I feel more connected with myself than I ever have before."

title: Jennifer Lopez reveals what makes a man 'sexy' to her

title: 'Resurrection of the Christ' writer reveals Mel Gibson's dark spiritual warning about 'Passion' follow-up
summary: Randall Wallace reveals Mel Gibson warned him that "Satan's going to come after you" before they began writing "The Resurrection of the Christ."
story: Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo calls out the ultimate threat to democracy in Los Angeles and dissects a musical glorifying accused United Healthcare CEO killer Luigi Mangione on The Ingraham Angle.
Mel Gibson's longtime collaborator Randall Wallace revealed the dark spiritual warning that the two-time Oscar winner gave him before they began writing the follow-up to "The Passion of the Christ."

The 76-year-old screenwriter, who previously teamed up with the 70-year-old director and actor for 1995's "Braveheart," 2002's "We Were Soldiers" and 2016's "Hacksaw Ridge," co-wrote the screenplay for "The Resurrection of the Christ" with Gibson and his brother Donal Gibson.

During a recent appearance on Raymond Arroyo's podcast "Arroyo Grande," Wallace recalled how he urged Gibson to tell the Resurrection story following the massive success of "The Passion of the Christ."
MEL GIBSON'S 'RESURRECTION OF THE CHRIST' REVEALS FIRST PHOTOS AFTER LONG-AWAITED PASSION FOLLOW-UP
"Mel didn't approach me. I approached him, actually," Wallace said of how they began working together on "The Resurrection of the Christ."

Mel Gibson's longtime collaborator revealed the stark warning that the director gave him before they began co-writing "The Resurrection of the Christ." (Domenico Cippitelli/NurPhoto via Getty Images; Elise Lockwood for Lionsgate)

"This is not to say that over the years, he hadn't thought many times about the Resurrection," Wallace continued. "In fact, in the original ‘The Passion of the Christ,’ the original cut didn't have the resurrection scene. He was getting feedback from people saying, 'We really want to see that.'"
Wallace said Gibson ultimately decided to add the brief Resurrection scene that serves as "The Passion of the Christ's" closing epilogue.
In the sequence, Jesus is seen rising, leaving the tomb, and revealing the wounds in his hands before the movie ends.
Randall Wallace co-wrote the follow-up to the 2004 mega-hit with Gibson and the director's brother Donal Gibson. (Mary Evans/Ronald Grant/Everett Collection)
Wallace told Arroyo that he proposed developing a feature-length film depicting the Resurrection while he and Gibson were on a promotional tour for "Hacksaw Ridge" in 2016.

"Having studied the Resurrection and being so consumed by it, I thought about it many times," Wallace recalled. "I didn't have anything to do with ‘The Passion of the Christ.’ When we were promoting ‘Hacksaw Ridge,’ we were sitting there talking about our lives, and I said, ‘Look, you know, the story that you really need to tell is the Resurrection.’"
Wallace went on to recount Gibson's reaction to his suggestion, remembering that the director believed the project could invite spiritual warfare.
Wallace recalled that Gibson warned him, "Satan's going to come after you." (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images)

"There was this long pause, and he said something profoundly beautiful. He said, 'If we do this, it can't be for the money, and it can't be to get back at people that have hated us or wronged us or been unhappy with us,'" Wallace recalled. "And I said, ‘Amen to that.’"
"Then he said, 'You know, Satan's going to come after you,'" Wallace continued.
"I said, 'Well, you know, Satan doesn't really care about Baptists.' It's really good when Satan can get a Catholic. We're a dime a dozen," he said as Arroyo laughed.
"And of course, I was being facetious, but I was also thinking…" Wallace continued.
"What if he's right?" Arroyo interjected.
"Well, yeah," Wallace admitted.
"That's what I would be thinking," Arroyo said.
"We had a beautiful conversation about grace," Wallace recalled.
Wallace said he pitched Gibson on the follow-up when they were promoting 2016's "Hacksaw Ridge." (Mike Marsland/Mike Marsland/WireImage via Getty Images)
Wallace told Arroyo that conversation with Gibson marked the beginning of their collaboration on "The Resurrection of the Christ."

"I knew he had written ‘The Passion,’ was very much deeply involved in the writing of it. And I said, 'Look, let's partner up. I'll write a draft, give it to you, then we'll start tearing it up, go through it. You do your thing, I'll do mine. We'll work together, we'll work apart.' So we started that way," Wallace remembered.
Gibson has previously said he, Wallace and Donal spent roughly six to eight years writing and refining the screenplay for "The Resurrection of the Christ," which will be split into two parts.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

In May, Gibson announced that production on the follow-up had been completed. "The Resurrection of the Christ: Part One" will be released May 6, 2027, on Ascension Day, the Christian holiday marking Jesus Christ’s ascent into heaven 40 days after Easter Sunday. "The Resurrection of the Christ: Part Two" is scheduled to debut May 25, 2028, over Memorial Day weekend.
Jaakko Ohtonen is starring as Jesus in "The Resurrection of the Christ: Part One." (Elise Lockwood for Lionsgate)
In a press release, Gibson shared that the story was brought to the screen "exactly as I envisioned it."
"I’m deeply grateful to my incredibly talented cast and crew for pouring their hearts into this production. Together, we created something powerful," Gibson said.

"This film represents a major part of my life’s work, and it has demanded everything of me as a filmmaker and as an artist. This is far more than a film to me. It’s a mission I’ve carried for over 20 years to tell what I believe is the most important story in human history," he added.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"The Passion of the Christ," which premiered in February 2004, depicted the final 12 hours of Jesus’ life leading up to the crucifixion. Its graphic violence and subject matter made it one of that year's most controversial movies.
The film was a smash hit, grossing more than $610 million worldwide on a reported $30 million budget. It also earned Academy Award nominations for its makeup, score and cinematography.
"The Passion of the Christ" starred Jim Caviezel as Jesus of Nazareth. (Lionsgate/Fathom Entertainment)
While speaking with Arroyo, Wallace teased what audiences can expect from the long-awaited follow-up.
"His unique vision of the spiritual realm is really special," Wallace said of Gibson.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"The interesting thing is that, while in some ways — the ultimate movie — I want to keep it all secret about what's going to happen," he continued. "But the ultimate movie, in some ways, will have elements that people have never seen before."

"In fact, in many ways, it'll be stuff nobody's ever seen," Wallace added. "And yet I believe it'll be, in a certain way, the most orthodox telling. It'll be the most consistent telling of the overall belief, the awe and the mystery that Christians experience when they experience the Resurrection."
Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: Helen Mirren re-lists historic Hollywood Hills estate after $6.5M price slash
summary: Helen Mirren and Taylor Hackford's 6.5-acre compound, built in 1911 for a silent film star, carries over a century of Old Hollywood legacy.
story: Helen Mirren reflected on the secret behind her chemistry with her co-stars Harrison Ford and Pierce Brosnan. Mirren previously starred with Ford in the Western drama "1923" and she is currently playing Brosnan's wife in the new series "MobLand."
A piece of Hollywood history is looking for its next owner.

Oscar-winning actress Helen Mirren and her husband, acclaimed director Taylor Hackford, are putting their longtime Hollywood Hills estate on the market for $12 million, offering buyers a rare chance to own a property steeped in more than a century of entertainment history.
The couple first listed the property in 2021 for $18.5 million before reducing the asking price.
DIANE KEATON'S FORMER LA HOME HITS THE MARKET AT $22.9M MONTHS AFTER HER DEATH
Helen Mirren's 10,199-square-foot estate is on the market for $12 million. (Marc Angeles/Vesta Home)
Spanning 6.5 acres, the approximately 10,199-square-foot compound is far more than a luxury home — it is a surviving piece of Old Hollywood.
An outdoor dining patio overlooks a swimming pool, landscaped grounds and a city skyline beyond. (Marc Angeles/Vesta Home)

Built in 1911 for silent film star Dustin Farnum, the estate has passed through the hands of several notable figures over the decades, including film producer and journalist Mark Hellinger and actress-producer Gail Patrick, who served as executive producer of the original "Perry Mason" television series.
A wood-paneled library includes built-in bookshelves, a fireplace and contemporary furnishings. (Marc Angeles/Vesta Home)
Vesta Home staged the interiors with a design that walks the line between nostalgia and modern luxury, honoring the home’s cinematic past without turning it into a museum.

Deep silk rugs, rich green tones, warm wood accents, vintage furnishings and oversized black-and-white Hollywood photography fill the grand-scale rooms, creating spaces that feel both glamorous and inviting.
A bathroom includes a soaking tub, glass-block shower enclosure and dual-sink vanity. (Marc Angeles/Vesta Home)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

The private compound features a grand main residence, a separate three-bedroom guesthouse, an office and apartment above the garage, a swimming pool, sweeping terraces and newly refreshed landscaping surrounded by mature trees and panoramic Hollywood Hills views.
A landscaped swimming pool offers elevated views overlooking palm trees and the surrounding city skyline. (Marc Angeles/Vesta Home)

"This is a truly rare opportunity to acquire one of the Hollywood Hills' most historically significant and private estates," said listing agent Jonas Heller. "Properties of this caliber, with such a rich legacy and expansive acreage, seldom become available."
A bright kitchen includes white cabinetry, marble countertops and expansive windows overlooking greenery. (Marc Angeles/Vesta Home)
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
The property is exclusively listed by Jonas Heller and Kurt Rappaport of Westside Estate Agency.
Helen Mirren and her husband Taylor Hackford tied the knot in 1997. (Michael Tran/AFP)
Hackford, the former president of the Directors Guild of America, has been married to Mirren since 1997.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Hollywood actress is known for her roles in "The Queen," "1923," "MobLand" and more. She previously told Fox News Digital what surprised her about working with co-stars Pierce Brosnan and Harrison Ford.
"I think with both of them, as I say, it's the way they behave on set, professionally," Mirren said.

"Harrison would sit around and chat with the cowboys," she added. "And it was cold, it wasn't comfortable. He didn't go off to his trailer and sit in a nice, warm, comfortable trailer. He would sit in the cold with everybody else. You know, chatting to the guys, for example."
WATCH: ‘MOBLAND’ STAR HELEN MIRREN CALLS OUT ‘GRUMPY’ RICH ACTORS

"And Pierce — Pierce just is so great. And you know what the other thing is great about them both? They both love what they do. And I've noticed, in my profession, a lot of older actors kind of get grumpy. Actresses don't, but actors do.

"They get grumpy, and I think, what the — excuse my language — f--- do you have to be grumpy about? You're working, you've been paid a lot of money, everyone's looking after you. Well, what do you got to be grumpy about? Harrison and Pierce are so not grumpy. They're just — they love what they do. They're positive about it. It's what they do, and they love it."
Mirren has won five Emmy Awards, an Academy Award and a Tony Award. She has also won four BAFTAs and three Golden Globes.
Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment writer for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Breakfast Club' star Anthony Michael Hall reveals the key to surviving Hollywood after 51 years
summary: Anthony Michael Hall reveals the secret to his 51-year Hollywood career and draws parallels between "Breakfast Club" and "Nation's Dumbest."
story: Anthony Michael Hall told Fox News Digital that you have to have "thick skin" to survive in Hollywood.
"Breakfast Club" star Anthony Michael Hall knows exactly why he's been able to survive Hollywood for over 50 years.
Hall is starring on the FOX celebrity competition series "Nation's Dumbest," hosted by Jack Whitehall. At the press event, Hall explained the secret to longevity in Hollywood.

"Having a thick skin, and just being game and just wanting to work with the best people you can," he began. "Just being persistent and tenacious. And thank God I was born with a hard head. But you have to have a thick skin."
Anthony Michael Hall starred in "The Breakfast Club." (Getty Images)
"You have to really want and love what you do. So I think that's it."
MATT DAMON SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S 'RUTHLESS' NATURE HAS TAKEN HIM AWAY FROM FATHERHOOD MORE THAN HE'D LIKE
Hall also told Fox News Digital the biggest lesson he's learned after five decades in the industry.
WATCH: 'Breakfast Club' star Anthony Michael Hall reveals the key to surviving Hollywood after 51 years

"Stay humble, stay focused, keep your eyes on the road, and just keep moving ahead somehow. There's no guarantees of anything in this business, and it's a tough business, but it's really great business, so I'm very fortunate," he noted.
Anthony Michael Hall poses for a portrait circa 1984. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
"[I] feel very blessed. This is my 51st year doing this, and this was really a unique thing, because it was something I never expected," Hall continued, referring to "Nation's Dumbest."

"It really took me by surprise, and it was really lot of fun," he said. "So, it was about learning that lesson, too. Staying open to new opportunities, just being cool with it and having fun. So, we really had a great time, all of us. It was nice."
WATCH: Dr. Drew and Andrew Yang reveal most frustrating part of 'Nation's Dumbest'

"Nation's Dumbest" is FOX's new celebrity competition series that puts a comedic twist on the traditional game show format. Hosted by Whitehall, the series challenges 12 celebrities to return to "summer school," where they compete in a mix of classroom-inspired trivia, physical games and school-themed challenges.
Anthony Michael Hall in 2021. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

But unlike most competition shows, the objective isn't to win — it's to be eliminated. Each week, the contestant who performs the best "graduates" from the competition, while those who struggle remain in the game. In the end, the last celebrity standing earns the title no one wants: "The Nation's Dumbest."
Hall told Fox News Digital that he saw some parallels from his days on the "Breakfast Club" and being back in a classroom setting on FOX's new competition series.
WATCH: JoJo Siwa and Chase Hudson talk competing on FOX's 'Nation's Dumbest'

"Do you know what, there was some parallels for sure. We all got thrown together. We're all stuck, we couldn't really go anywhere. And honestly, we all really got along. It was a real nice organic surprise that I had a great time with all these people. It was coming into a year where I wasn't sure where the next job was gonna come, like we often feel in this industry. And I got the call, and I was just really excited by it," he said.
"And I really embraced it and I just went up to Toronto and had a good time shooting it and everybody was really cool. So we had a really good time," Hall concluded.
Judd Nelson, Emilio Estevez, Ally Sheedy, Molly Ringwald and Anthony Michael Hall in "The Breakfast Club." (Universal Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection)
The inaugural cast includes Hall, Ice-T, Jon Heder, Hilaria Baldwin, Carmen Electra, Chase Hudson, Elle King, Matt Leinart, Dr. Drew Pinsky, Steve-O, JoJo Siwa and Andrew Yang.

title: Willie Robertson's faith-based advice that's kept his 34-year marriage to wife Korie strong
summary: Willie and Korie Robertson reveal the faith-based habits that have kept their 34-year marriage strong and inspired their new EKKL Entertainment platform.
story: "Duck Dynasty" stars Willie and Korie Robertson explained how they rely on biblical principles, shared purpose and a commitment to "stay on the same page" while building a business together.
"Duck Dynasty" stars Willie and Korie Robertson shared the faith-based marriage advice that has guided their lasting partnership.

The reality TV personalities, who tied the knot in 1992, have spent more than three decades building a family, a multimillion-dollar business and a television empire together. Now, Willie, 54, and Korie, 52, have launched their latest joint venture, the faith-and-family media platform EKKL Entertainment.
During an interview with Fox News Digital, the couple, who are devout Christians, explained how they keep their marriage thriving despite the pressures of working together.
'DUCK DYNASTY' REVIVAL SHOWCASES WILLIE ROBERTSON'S NEW 'SEMI-RETIRED' LIFE
"I think Korie and I pull back to our faith, which is very important," Willie said. "We believe in something bigger than us."
"Duck Dynasty" star Willie and Korie Robertson share the faith-based advice that guides their 34-year marriage. (Korie Robertson Instagram)

"The aspects of it are love and joy and peace and patience, kindness, that's helpful. Gentleness. I mean, all these things are that's the core of our faith," he continued. "And so those are the things that we try to implement. Not just with everybody else in our life, but we implemented that in our marriage as well. And we try to treat each other like that as well."
Willie noted that he and Korie had seen successful and unsuccessful relationships and intentionally chosen the practices they wanted to emulate.

"We've had great examples of that in our families, from our parents to other people to where we see how that works," he explained. "We also see things that don't, and we see people that can get themselves in a bad way, and then their marriage falls apart. And we've seen that."

"Not just in Hollywood or people that we know that are famous," Willie added. "We see it up and down our street here, you know, like, like you don't have to be bad to start bickering with each other and fighting and let things go in."

Willie pointed to simple habits that the couple has adopted throughout their 34-year marriage. He explained that putting their faith into practice means approaching their relationship with patience, kindness and grace while making a conscious effort to resolve conflicts before they grow.

"Those are the things we do — things we've learned from our faith," Willie said. "Not going to bed while you're angry. I mean, these are just things that you put into your life and say, ‘Oh, this is helpful.’ And so I think that's part of things we do to keep drawn together and keep being together on the same page."
Korie shared how the couple live out their faith, explaining that it is the lens through which the Robertsons approach marriage, parenting and work.

"I would say our faith informs everything we do," she said. "It's not just like what we do on Sunday morning at church or whatever. It's how we parent, how we are as husband and wife, how we're as coworkers and all that. So it informs everything."
Korie noted that their shared sense of purpose is also what led the couple to launch their latest venture together.

"I think it's exciting to be on a mission together," she said. "Like we are, as a family, we are on our mission together to spread the love of Jesus and let people know about him. And so we can do that in — any of us can do that in a hundred thousand different ways."

"For us, for our family, it is through entertainment and God has kind of put us in this position to get to do it," Korie added. "And so we keep just saying yes and opening the door whenever someone knocks, I guess."
The couple married in 1992 and share six children. (Michael Buckner/ACM2015/Getty Images for dcp)
Though Willie and Korie grew up in the same West Monroe, Louisiana, community, the couple noted that they came from very different worlds.
JESSIE JAMES DECKER ON WHY HER MARRIAGE TO ERIC DECKER HASN'T LOST ITS SPARK AFTER FOUR KIDS
"I grew up in a neighborhood. I was a yuppie," Korie said with a laugh.
"I grew up really poor on the end of a dead-end dirt road," Willie recalled.

The pair first met as elementary school students at a Christian summer camp in Louisiana. Though Willie went to public school while Korie attended private school, the two continued to see each other through church youth group and around the West Monroe area.
Willie and Korie, who now share six children, began dating seriously after high school and married less than a year later.
Korie told Fox News Digital that despite their different backgrounds, they found commonality in the values their families shared.

"I think for us, it's like the externals did look very different growing up," she said. "We definitely looked very different. His dad had a big beard and wore camo and my dad actually had a little beard. It was a manicured beard and wore a suit, you know?"

Korie continued, "And so from the externals, it looked different, but the things that were important actually looked the same. Faith first and foremost, hospitality, generosity, kindness to strangers are to your neighbor. Like, those things."
Willie said that he believed their contrasting backgrounds have ultimately strengthened both their marriage and their business partnership by giving them complementary perspectives and skill sets.
"Actually, it has been helpful," he explained. "You think about all the stuff men ever do, like the perspective I have of country people, poor people, you know. Like that's how I grew up."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Willie and Korie reflected on how coming from different backgrounds strengthens their partnership. (Bryan Tarnowski/A&E 2026 )

"You come from a business world where your family was successful in business," he told Korie. "You had to figure out how to build things, build businesses, build retail business. So I think when you bring that together, it's powerful."
"There's not as many blind spots," Willie continued. "Like if we both had come from the same neighborhood, there would obviously be some blind spots."
Willie and Korie recalled the major ice storm that hit Louisiana in late January 2026, which left many residents, including them, without power for several days.

The duo explained that they relied on each other's strengths including Willie's hunting and fishing skills and Korie's business acumen, to help their family get through the outage and deal with the aftermath.
"When the ice storm happened, and we had no electricity, we needed him to help us survive," Korie said.
"Nobody was worried," Willie said. "We were going to eat and figure it out."
"And I could read the contracts," Korie added as the two laughed.
"The insurance law, you know, the claims on what we're gonna have to turn in the insurance, which I never would have figured out," Willie said.
"That's how our stuff works," Korie noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
While speaking with Fox News Digital, Willie and Korie shared the inspiration behind their new venture, EKKL.

The Robertsons explained that raising their six children in the spotlight opened their eyes to media consumption, but it was seeing their young grandchildren mimic movie lines and songs in real time that made them realize just how much the content they were watching was impacting and shaping them.

Korie explained that this observation led them to create EKKL, which is a faith-based entertainment platform that they describe as a "one-stop shop" for families seeking trusted movies, TV shows, podcasts, children's content and daily devotionals.

"It is definitely part of us coming in to try to help solve a problem that I think all families are having right now," she said. "Like, what is the safe space for our kids to consume entertainment? There's so much out there. There are so many access points to our kids' hearts and minds. And, you know, how do we protect that in them?"
"And also, how do we find good content for us as adults?" Korie added.
The Robertsons said they believe there is an untapped appetite for faith-and family-centered storytelling, arguing that Hollywood has underestimated what audiences want to watch.

"I think when you're talking about faith and you're a family — those are things that bring us back together," Willie said. "I think part of the problem with Hollywood is they're not — they don't know what to put out. They're like, ‘Oh, this group may not like this’ and we're all in a family, you know? And these are stories that can pull us hopefully back together."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I would say there is room in Hollywood for it," Korie said. "And we've proven over and over again that that's what people want to see. But unfortunately, sometimes the perception is that, ‘Oh, it has to be trashy’ or it have all this like content in it to be successful.' When we're saying like, wait, maybe that's just because that's what you're advertising, that's you're giving us, that's that you're putting out there."
"But if we offered something else to people, maybe they would prove to us that that's actually what they want."
Ashley Hume is an entertainment journalist for Fox News Digital and Fox Business who covers breaking news, celebrity culture, major industry events and the business of entertainment.

title: Original 'Little House' villain returns for reboot with warning for new Nellie
summary: Alison Arngrim reveals her surprise cameo in Netflix's "Little House on the Prairie" reboot and shares advice for the new Nellie Oleson actress.
story: Actor Warren Christie tells Fox News Digital about his role in the upcoming Netflix adaptation and why the series will appeal to old fans while bringing in new audiences.
Alison Arngrim is back on the prairie.
The actress who made Nellie Oleson one of television's most unforgettable villains returns with a surprise cameo in Netflix's new "Little House on the Prairie" reboot, now streaming.
Although she hasn't met Willa Dunn, the child actress taking over the iconic role, Arngrim already has some hard-earned advice on how to perfect the art of playing the girl everyone loves to hate.
'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' RETURNS AS NEW NETFLIX ADAPTATION AIMS FOR WHOLESOME ENTERTAINMENT

Alison Arngrim played the unforgettable Nellie Oleson on NBC's "Little House on the Prairie" for all nine seasons, from 1974 to 1983, becoming one of television's most iconic young villains. (Getty Images)
The actress is also reuniting with her former castmates in Nashville from Sept. 11-13, 2026. They will be at the famous Grand Ole Opry on Sept. 11, 2026.

"You've got to have a solid sense of who you are," the actress told Fox News Digital. "It's a tall order for someone who's like 10, 11 or 12 years old, but when people are talking about this other person who lived in the 1800s, saying, 'I hate her so much. She's so awful. I can't stand her. I want to slap her in the face,' you can't take that personally."
The original "Little House on the Prairie" series has cultivated a devoted following, affectionately known as "Bonnetheads." (Eric Fougere/Corbis via Getty Images)
"You cannot think it's real — that people want to slap you in the face or that you did something wrong. It's actually a compliment. It means you're doing it right."
Actress Alison Arngrim poses during a photocall for the series "Little House on the Prairie" at the 63rd Monte-Carlo Television Festival in Monaco on June 15, 2024. (Valery Hache/AFP)

"Remember, Sir Anthony Hopkins didn't lose sleep over being Hannibal Lecter," she said. "You are who you are, and this is just a character. You have to understand the job is to irritate, annoy and upset people. And if you do it correctly with a character like Nellie, people are going to be annoyed. But when someone says, 'I can't stand her,' you can't possibly take that in."
WATCH: NETFLIX'S ‘LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE’ ACTOR HOPES NEW SERIES WILL UNITE OLD AND NEW FANS
Arngrim was more than ready to become a despised villain. Raised in a family of actors and performing since she was 5 years old, she viewed every "I hate you" from fans as the ultimate applause.
From left: Melissa Gilbert as Laura Elizabeth Ingalls Wilder and Alison Arngrim as Nellie Oleson in "Little House on the Prairie." (NBCU Photo Bank)

"I've had people come up to me and go, 'You were a complete b----, and I hated you. You were absolutely hideous and revolting. I was terrified of you,'" she said with a laugh. "I just said, 'Oh my God, thank you so much. You're too kind.' It's a weird thing, but you have to understand the character has nothing to do with you. It's someone who has nothing to do with you."
And fans haven't let her forget it.

More than 40 years after "Little House on the Prairie" ended, Alison Arngrim says many fans still can't separate her from Nellie Oleson — proof that one of television's most notorious mean girls never really left Walnut Grove. (Eric Fougere/Corbis via Getty Images)

"I still remember when someone threw a McDonald's cup of orange soda at my face during a Christmas parade," she said. "I think people are a little more sane today, or they understand fantasy a little better now."
Arngrim has no regrets about playing television's most infamous bully.

Alison Arngrim turned "Nasty Nellie" into one of television's most iconic villains — a role that still follows her decades after "Little House on the Prairie." (NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal/Getty Images)

"I got the joke," she said. "I knew you were supposed to hate me, and I was fine with it. But it's really weird because I'm 64 years old, and I still have people yelling at me about all the things I did to Laura 52 years ago. Some people are still really mad, and that's very bizarre. So I will tell the new Nellie to brace herself. But she also has to understand that if she does it right, people will absolutely hate her. And if she really does it right, they'll love her too."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Willa Dunn will play Nellie Oleson in Netflix's "Little House" reboot. (Theo Wargo/Getty Images for Phiphen Studios)
Arngrim was asked to make her cameo about two weeks before production was set to film her scene.

"I play this very strange woman in the woods," she said. "I used to have Marilyn Monroe's makeup guy every morning, who made sure we looked really nice. But when I first sat down in the makeup chair this time around, the makeup artist said, 'We're going to make you look so awful. I feel bad. You have such amazing skin. I'm going to totally ruin that.'"
Alison Arngrim as Ida appears with Andrea Greening in Netflix's "Little House on the Prairie." (Eric Zachanowich/Netflix)
"They ruined everything," she said with a laugh. "They painted my teeth — my dentist is going to be horrified. They used colors like blood, tobacco and dirt."
Alison Arngrim is seen here in Netflix's "Little House on the Prairie." (Eric Zachanowich/Netflix)
Arngrim said that if original showrunner Michael Landon were alive, he would be "fascinated" by the new technology available in Hollywood today to help bring the "Little House" stories to life.
"I also think he would have Pa take off his shirt more often," she joked.
Michael Landon would give the Netflix reboot his blessing, Alison Arngrim told Fox News Digital. (NBCU Photo Bank)

"But Michael somehow knew that 'Little House' would stand the test of time," she said. "He used to tell everyone on set that everyone's going to be watching this after we're all gone. He predicted that. And here we are. I think he would be so impressed that the show is being retold again. I also think he would want to direct every single episode, and he would have lots to say because he was very picky."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Michael Landon on the set of "Little House on the Prairie," circa 1974. The drama, adapted from the novels by Laura Ingalls Wilder (1867-1957), starred Landon as Charles "Pa" Ingalls. (Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images)
Today, Arngrim hopes she'll soon meet the new Nellie. She's also urging skeptical fans to give Netflix's reboot a chance.
Alison Arngrim told Fox News Digital she quickly befriended the cast of Netflix's "Little House on the Prairie." (Eric Zachanowich/Netflix)
"How many 'Star Treks' do we have now?" she said. "A lot. And remember, when our show first aired, some people said, 'No, it can only be the books.' These actors get it. The cast is fabulous."
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP

The cast of "Little House on the Prairie" with a dog, mid 1970s, from left, Melissa Gilbert, Michael Landon (1936-1991), Karen Grassle, who holds an unidentified baby, Melissa Sue Anderson, and Lindsay or Sidney Greenbush. (Fotos International/Getty Images)

"There's just something special about these stories," Arngrim said. "If I close my eyes, I can hear Michael laughing, with his high-pitched giggle. Who would have thought 'Little House' would still be around today? Well, Michael did. 'Little House' is never going away."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: 'Growing Pains' child star Ashley Johnson reveals 'dark' moment armed fan tried to abduct her from set
summary: Ashley Johnson details the moment an armed audience member lunged from the crowd and grabbed her during a "Growing Pains" live taping in the early '90s.
story: Jeremy Miller detailed a challenging sobriety setback on his road to recovery from alcoholism.
Ashley Johnson is recalling a terrifying moment from her childhood in Hollywood, revealing a fan grabbed her and tried to abduct her during a live taping of "Growing Pains."

The former child star says she was just 7 years old when an armed fan broke from a studio audience line, grabbed her and tried to carry her away during a live taping after production had received a threat warning that someone planned to bring a gun to the set. Johnson said the man was armed.
"It was in the first year that I was on, and we had only done a couple of film nights," Johnson began on the "Weird Kids" podcast.
KIRK CAMERON PRAISES NASHVILLE'S 'GOOD VALUES' AFTER DITCHING CALIFORNIA OVER COST OF LIVING, POLITICS

The child star behind Chrissy Seaver, Ashley Johnson, reveals how lax security on the "Growing Pains" set led to a terrifying kidnapping attempt by an armed fan. (Christopher Polk/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images)
Back then, she said, security around the cast was far less restrictive than it is today.

"So, I hadn't done that many yet… and at that time, all of the cast sort of had trailers, and they were like old camper trailers," Johnson said. "Like they're not like the fancy trailers that they are now."
Ashley Johnson says an armed man grabbed her during a live taping of "Growing Pains" when she was 7, after production received a chilling threat. (Walt Disney Television/Getty Images)
She explained that cast members walked directly past audience members on their way into the studio.
"We would exit our trailers before the shoot and the audience that would be walking in, you would walk by the audience before you would walk into the studio," she said.
"And this is going to get a little dark, but somebody had written in and said that ‘I am coming to set, and I am going to bring a gun… I am going to murder some of the cast.’"

This 1991 image released by ABC shows the cast of "Growing Pains," including Leonardo DiCaprio, Alan Thicke, Jeremy Miller, Kirk Cameron, Joanna Kerns, Tracey Gold and Ashley Johnson. (Bob D'Amico/ABC)
With audience members only "within five feet" away when the cast was walking into the studio, Johnson said one man suddenly lunged toward her.

"So, I'm walking with my mom, and then I just remember some guy hops out of the line, and he grabs me… grabs me up and starts booking it," she said. "And all I remember is like, there was security that somehow got on him after some time."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Johnson pointed out that she was too young to grasp the danger.
She remembered "flying around in the air" as security wrestled the suspect to the ground.
BROOKE SHIELDS REFLECTS ON BEING MADE A 'SEX SYMBOL' AT A YOUNG AGE AND HOW SHE TURNED THE PAGE ON FAME

title: Ricky Gervais rejects calls to tone down comedy: 'Be offended if you want'
summary: Ricky Gervais says backlash only makes his jokes funnier, revealing why he's finally done addressing cancel culture in his stand-up tours now.
story: Raymond Arroyo is here with a special Thursday edition of Seen and Unseen.
Ricky Gervais isn't backing away from controversial comedy.

The comedian doubled down on his long-held defense of free speech during a recent radio interview, saying he has no interest in changing his material to avoid offending audiences and arguing that backlash only adds to the joke.
"I don't tell people not to be offended; I tell them I don't care if they are. Be offended if you want, it makes it funnier for me," Gervais said during an appearance on BBC Radio 2.
RICKY GERVAIS MOCKS GRAMMY WINNERS MAKING POLITICAL SPEECHES, SAYS THEY'RE 'STILL NOT LISTENING'
Ricky Gervais speaks onstage at the Season 3 Premiere of Netflix's "After Life" at the BFI Southbank in London.  (David M. Benett/Dave Benett/Getty Images, File)

The 65-year-old comic, whose stand-up specials have frequently sparked criticism over jokes about politics, gender identity, religion and celebrities, rejected the idea that he intentionally sets out to provoke audiences.

"You can't help by what you're offended by, but … don't expect me to care. … It's a myth that I go out to offend. I never go out to offend," he said. "I just know that it's probably going to happen because everyone's different."
Gervais argued that virtually any opinion can offend someone.
RICKY GERVAIS SAYS HE HAD A 'BLAST' AT THE GOLDEN GLOBES: 'MAKE JOKES, NOT WAR'
Ricky Gervais at the 2012 Golden Globes (Paul Drinkwater/NBC via Getty Images, File)
"There's nothing you can say, particularly anything that's mildly interesting or contentious or your viewpoint, that someone somewhere won't find offensive," he said.
Reflecting on how reactions to comedy have evolved, Gervais said audiences today are quicker to take offense than they were two decades ago.
"And times have changed. Twenty years ago, if someone said I was offended by that, I probably would go, 'Why?' Now I go … 'I know you are. Everyone is.'"
Ricky Gervais tells the Los Angeles Times how he gets away with his offensive comedy. (Getty Images, File)
While Gervais has frequently addressed cancel culture and free speech in recent stand-up tours, he suggested he is ready to move on from the topic.
"I've dealt with it too much, actually. I think the last couple of tours, I have dealt with cancel culture and free speech because I felt I had to. Now, I don't have to," he said.
"I'm ignoring it all. I shouldn't even bring it into the room. Those people there who've paid hundreds of pounds — they're not offended. I can play to a million people, not one complaint."
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Ricky Gervais at the 2020 Golden Globes in Los Angeles (Paul Drinkwater/NBCUniversal via Getty Images, File)
Gervais insisted the outrage over his comedy doesn't come from the crowds filling his shows. It comes after his specials reach a much bigger audience online.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
"As soon as it goes on Netflix, 50 million people. Of course, there's going to be someone who doesn't like it. What am I going to do? It's too late. I've been paid."
The comic has long dismissed calls to tone down his material, repeatedly defending free speech and arguing that comedians shouldn't shy away from controversial subjects.

Earlier this year, Gervais reignited debate by reposting one of the most memorable lines from his 2020 Golden Globes opening monologue, taking another swipe at celebrities who use awards shows as political platforms.

"If you do win an award tonight, don't use it as a platform to make a political speech," Gervais told the star-studded crowd. "You're in no position to lecture the public about anything. You know nothing about the real world. Most of you spent less time in school than Greta Thunberg."
Reposting the quote on X, Gervais added a jab of his own: "They're still not listening."
