University of Basel researchers are developing MIR, a tiny dental robot designed to help prepare teeth for crowns with digital precision. (University of Basel, Catherine Weyer)
Why crowns take more than one dental visit

If tooth decay leaves a large cavity, a dentist may need to prepare the tooth for a crown. Today, that can mean several steps. The dentist removes decay, fills the cavity, shapes the tooth, takes an impression and fits a temporary crown. Then, the permanent crown gets made and placed during a later visit.

That is where MIR could help. The goal is to move more of the process into a digital workflow. After a scan, a dentist could plan how much tooth material the robot should remove. Then, the crown could be ordered right away instead of waiting for another appointment.
How the tiny dental robot works
MIR attaches to a custom-fitted dental splint made from the patient's scan. That splint connects the robot to the teeth. So, if the patient turns their head, the robot moves with them.
That detail stood out to me. Anyone who has ever tried to stay perfectly still in a dental chair knows how hard that can be. Even a small twitch can feel huge when a drill is near your tooth.

The robot is designed to follow a digital treatment plan. In testing, it prepared tooth models in two stages. First, it used a wider drill to reduce the top of the tooth surface. Then, a longer, thinner drill worked along the sides.
HUMANOID ROBOTS PERFORM LIVE SURGERY IN WORLD FIRST
How small is MIR?

The University of Basel says the MIR prototype is about the size of a wine cork. It measures 43 by 26 by 28 millimeters. Dr. Yukiko Tomooka, the paper's first author, said the robot was designed to fit comfortably inside an open mouth.

That small size is key. A dental robot cannot feel bulky or block the dentist's view. It also cannot depend on a giant device sitting inside your mouth. So, the Basel team moved the larger parts outside the mouth and kept the in-mouth unit compact.

The project page from the University of Basel's Department of Biomedical Engineering says the team wants MIR to enable a fully digital treatment workflow for tooth preparation. The long-term vision is a crown that can be manufactured before or during the preparation process using CAD-CAM dental technology.
Researchers say the miniature dental robot has been tested on synthetic tooth models and dental-like ceramic materials. (University of Basel, Catherine Weyer)
How precise is the dental robot?

So far, MIR has been tested on tooth models made of synthetic resin and on ceramic material with hardness similar to tooth enamel. In those tests, the robot's positional error was less than 0.2 millimeters, even though the current version does not yet have sensors to directly measure or correct its position.

Researchers also measured the force created during drilling. University of Basel says the forces stayed below five newtons, which it compares to the gravitational force of a half-liter bottle of water. The team is also studying the robot's noise level to better understand how it might work in a real dental office.
Why MIR still has a long road ahead

This tiny robot has not yet reached dental offices. University of Basel says more work is needed before MIR can be used in dental practices. The next step is to add sensors and a camera, so the system can track its position and monitor the treatment as it happens.

That safety piece is a big deal. The team wants MIR to know where it is, even after a power outage. Professor Georg Rauter, who leads the research group, said the goal is for the robot to continue from the right position using sensor data.

In other words, the robot needs better awareness before anyone should trust it near a real tooth. Precision on models is one thing. A real mouth adds saliva, movement, pressure, nerves and patient anxiety.
Who is behind the tiny dental robot?
MIR was developed by researchers at the Department of Biomedical Engineering at the University of Basel. The idea came from researchers at the University of Zurich, who also took part in the work.

The University of Basel project page lists the BIROMED-Lab, the Clinic of Reconstructive Dentistry at the University of Zurich, Camlog Biotechnologies and the University of Bern's ARTORG Center as collaborators. The project is sponsored by Innosuisse. The research was published in IEEE Transactions on Medical Robotics and Bionics.
BIONIC HANDS ARE NOW TEACHING ROBOTS TO FEEL
MIR remains a prototype, with researchers planning to add sensors and a camera before testing it in real dental settings. (University of Basel, Catherine Weyer)
What this means for you
If you have ever needed a crown, you know the process can drag on. MIR could eventually make that experience faster by letting dentists scan, plan and prepare the tooth with more digital precision.

Still, this technology remains in development. You should not expect a tiny robot to show up at your next dental appointment. Researchers still need to add sensors, add a camera and prove that the system can work safely in real treatment settings.

Even so, this is worth watching. Dentistry is already moving toward digital scans, computer-designed crowns and more guided procedures. A robot like MIR could push that trend further, especially if it can reduce repeat visits.
Kurt's key takeaways

This is the kind of dental tech that makes you lean forward and squirm a little. A tiny robot mounted inside your mouth may sound intense. Still, the goal is something many of us would welcome: fewer follow-up appointments when a crown is needed. The most important detail is that MIR remains a prototype. It has only been tested on models and dental-like materials so far. The team still plans to add sensors and a camera before real dental use. If MIR works, a future crown appointment could feel more like a guided digital procedure than the drawn-out process many of us know today.

title: Tesla helped save a driver; is your car ready?
summary: John Brandt's son used the Tesla app to reroute his father's Model Y to a hospital during a heart attack, but preparation made the difference.
story: It’s Distracted Driver Awareness Month, and automakers like GM are putting a focus on high-tech solutions to keep drivers safe behind the wheel.
A medical emergency behind the wheel is terrifying because every second suddenly feels bigger. You are trying to stay calm, stay safe and get help before things spiral.

That is why John Brandt's story is getting so much attention. His Tesla Model Y helped keep him moving during a heart attack, while his son used the Tesla app to reroute the car to a nearby emergency room.
The bigger takeaway isn’t that your car can replace 911. It cannot. The lesson is that connected-car settings, trusted app access and emergency contacts should be ready before you ever need them.
BEFORE YOU CONNECT ANOTHER SMART TV, TABLET OR PHONE, LOCK IT DOWN
A Tesla Model Y helped keep John Brandt moving toward help after chest pain hit during an early morning highway drive. (Tesla)
Free live CyberGuy class: Sick of Spam? Join us July 22

Join us Wednesday, July 22, at 1 p.m. ET for a free CyberGuy Live class that will help you cut down on robocalls, spam texts, junk email and other unwanted messages. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will walk you step by step through simple ways to filter spam, clean up your inbox and recognize the messages that could put your personal information at risk. How a Tesla Model Y helped during a medical emergency
Brandt said he was driving from Atlanta to Birmingham on I-20 around 4 a.m. when severe chest pain made it unsafe for him to keep driving on his own.
His Model Y had Full Self-Driving Supervised enabled, which helped keep the car on course while he called his son, Jack.

Jack then acted from his own phone. Because he was an authorized driver on his father's Tesla account, he could send a new destination to the vehicle through the Tesla app. He found Tanner Medical Center in Carrollton, Georgia and rerouted the car there.

He also called ahead, so emergency room staff knew a possible heart attack patient was coming. Brandt later said doctors found three blocked arteries and told him the fast reroute likely saved his life.
Brandt credited his family, the hospital team and Tesla's technology for helping him survive. His experience also shows why trusted access should be set up before a crisis starts.
Why the Tesla FSD medical emergency feels so personal

This story hits home because it sounds like something that could happen to any of us. You may be driving to help a parent. You may be on a highway before sunrise. You may think you feel heartburn or stress until the pain gets worse.

Most of us think about car safety in terms of brakes, airbags and tires. However, this story shows that app access, navigation settings and trusted contacts can also play a role in a crisis. That does not mean your car becomes a paramedic. It means your connected vehicle can give your family more ways to help if something goes wrong.
Brandt's experience raises a question every driver should consider: If you suddenly could not manage the trip alone, would someone you trust know how to step in and help?
How Tesla owners can prepare for a medical emergency

If you own a Tesla, start with trusted driver access. Add someone you trust completely, such as a spouse, adult child or close family member. Tesla lets owners add drivers through the Tesla app. Once added, that person may be able to access key vehicle features from a phone.
Choose carefully. A trusted driver may be able to see your vehicle location and use important app controls. That access can help in an emergency, but it also deserves serious thought.
TESLA ROBOTAXI MIAMI LAUNCH COMES WITH LIMITS
Next, show that person how to send a destination to your Tesla. Do not make this something they figure out during a crisis. Sit in the parked car and test it together.
Have them send a familiar destination to the vehicle. Make sure you both understand what appears on the screen. Then talk through what they should do if you ever call and say something is wrong.

Also save useful locations in your navigation system. Add home, work and hospitals you would likely use. If you often drive between two cities, look at hospitals along that route before you need them.
Why Full Self-Driving Supervised isn’t an emergency plan

Tesla calls the system Full Self-Driving Supervised for a reason. The driver still needs to pay attention and stay ready to take over at any time. Brandt's experience shows how the technology and app connectivity helped during one frightening emergency. But a Tesla cannot replace 911, an ambulance or a trained medical team.

If you feel chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, lightheadedness or pain in your arm, back or jaw, treat it as an emergency. Pull over safely if you can. Call 911 immediately. Emergency responders can start care on the way to the hospital and alert the ER before you arrive.
The car’s connected navigation features allowed Brandt’s son to reroute the vehicle to the nearest emergency room from his own phone. (Tesla)
Your car may help your family find you or send a destination. Still, it should never delay a medical call.
How to prepare any connected car for an emergency

You do not need a Tesla to learn from this story. Many newer vehicles have connected apps, navigation tools, roadside assistance buttons or emergency calling features. First, remember this: Your car should never replace 911. If you are having a medical emergency, pull over safely if you can and call for help immediately. These steps are about giving your family extra ways to help, not replacing emergency responders.

Open your automaker's app and review what it can do. Look for vehicle location, shared driver access, remote lock controls, roadside assistance and navigation features. Then make sure your trusted contact can use the app if your car allows it. If the app requires a login, two-factor code or owner approval, handle that now. Also, check app access after you get a new phone. Permissions can change when you upgrade. Also, because vehicle apps can show location and control certain car features, use a strong unique password, store it in a password manager and turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) if available. Only give app access to someone you fully trust.

Make sure your vehicle app can use location services when needed. Also allow important notifications from the app so you do not miss alerts about your car. Ask your trusted contact to check the same settings on their phone. If they cannot see your vehicle, receive alerts or open the app quickly, they may not be able to help during a crisis.

Some vehicles let you send a destination from your phone to the dashboard. Others do not. Find out now. Sit in your parked car and send a destination from your phone. Then ask your trusted contact to try it if they have authorized access. This quick test can prevent confusion later. It also shows you what your car will display when a new destination arrives.

Many vehicles have an SOS button, emergency assistance button or roadside help button. Do not assume they all work the same way. Check your owner's manual or automaker app. Find out whether the button calls 911, a private call center or roadside assistance. Also, learn whether the system shares your vehicle location. That detail can be critical if you cannot explain where you are.

Your phone may help even more than your car. Add emergency contacts, fill out your Medical ID or emergency information and make sure your family can reach you even when Do Not Disturb is on. Apple says iPhone emergency contacts can receive a text and your location after an emergency call, while Samsung lets Galaxy owners add emergency contacts, medical info and SOS sharing from Safety and emergency settings.

To make sure key people can reach you, go to Settings → Focus → Do Not Disturb → People and allow calls or notifications from your trusted contacts. You can also open a contact, tap Edit, choose Ringtone or Text Tone and turn on Emergency Bypass. Emergency Bypass can allow that person's calls or texts to come through even when Focus settings would normally silence them.

Open Settings

Choose your trusted contacts and tap Done

On Galaxy phones, also check Settings → Safety and emergency → Emergency Location Service and turn it on if available. This can help share your location with emergency responders in supported regions.

To let important calls through Do Not Disturb, go to Settings → Notifications → Do not disturb → Calls and messages or Allowed during Do not disturb, then allow favorite contacts or selected contacts. Favorite contacts can be allowed through while Do Not Disturb is on.

Technology can fail. Phones lose battery. Apps can lock you out. Keep a small emergency card in your wallet or glove box. Include emergency contacts, allergies, medications and your preferred hospital. If you have a heart condition or another medical concern, ask your doctor what details should be listed.

Trusted access should not be set once and forgotten. Remove anyone who no longer needs access to your vehicle app. Add someone new if your family situation changes. Also, update emergency contacts after a move, phone change or major health update.
Kurt's key takeaways

John Brandt's story is scary because it could happen to anyone. His Tesla helped, but the real lesson is preparation. If your car has an app, know what it can do before an emergency. Add a trusted family member, test the navigation tools and make sure your phone's emergency features are filled out. A car should never replace calling 911. However, the right setup can give your family one more way to help when every second counts.
If your car were involved in an emergency, would your family know what to do? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Apple AirDrop, Android Quick Share flaws put phones at risk
summary: Six new vulnerabilities in AirDrop and Quick Share could let nearby hackers exploit your phone in airports, coffee shops and crowded venues.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson warned of worrying privacy clauses in smart devices in a recent episode of the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share are the kind of phone features you probably use without thinking much about them. You want to send a photo across the room. You want to move a file from your phone to your laptop. So you tap share, pick a nearby device and move on.
Now, new security research shows those handy nearby-sharing tools can also create a wireless opening around your phone.

Researchers at the CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security examined Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share. They found six vulnerabilities across Apple, Samsung and Google implementations. The flaws include AirDrop crash bugs, Samsung Quick Share protocol issues and a Google Quick Share for Windows bug that could potentially lead to remote code execution.
BEFORE YOU CONNECT ANOTHER SMART TV, TABLET OR PHONE, LOCK IT DOWN
AirDrop and Quick Share make file sharing easy, but researchers say nearby sharing can also expose phones to wireless attacks in crowded places. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

That can affect you in a very everyday way. Your phone may be sitting in your pocket at an airport gate, in a coffee shop or inside a packed conference room while it listens for nearby sharing requests. If a bad actor gets close enough, they could try to take advantage of that open wireless doorway before you even realize anything happened. So, before you leave AirDrop or Quick Share open again, here is what the research found and the settings worth checking now.

Join us Wednesday, July 22, at 1 p.m. ET for a free CyberGuy Live class that will help you cut down on robocalls, spam texts, junk email and other unwanted messages. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will walk you step by step through simple ways to filter spam, clean up your inbox and recognize the messages that could put your personal information at risk. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our spam-stopping checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
AirDrop Quick Share security flaws explained

The researchers call this a proximity problem. AirDrop and Quick Share are built to find nearby devices without the usual setup of pairing first. That convenience is the whole point. It also means the sharing software has to listen before it fully trusts the other device.

According to the research, the affected protocols are used by more than five billion devices. Apple reports more than 2.2 billion active devices running the sharing service tied to AirDrop. Google reports more than 3 billion Android devices with Quick Share available system-wide or used as a default sharing tool on many phones.

The study found three AirDrop issues that could be triggered before authentication. It also found two Samsung Quick Share protocol flaws. In addition, researchers found one Google Quick Share for Windows use-after-free bug. Apple, Samsung and Google acknowledged the reports, according to the researchers.
Why AirDrop and Quick Share can expose your phone

Most phone attacks we talk about involve bad links, fake login pages or shady apps. This research points to a different kind of risk because it starts with physical proximity. A nearby attacker may not need your password. They may not need you to open a website either. In some cases, the target device only needs to be discoverable or in a sharing mode that listens for nearby devices.

That does not mean someone can grab every photo on your phone by standing next to you. The known flaws are narrower than that. Still, the research shows that file-sharing features sit closer to sensitive parts of the system than many of us realize. AirDrop interacts with Apple's sharing service, which supports features beyond file transfers. Quick Share also moves through low-level networking and device-to-device connection steps. That is why bugs in this area deserve your attention.
How nearby hackers could abuse AirDrop and Quick Share
The most immediate risk is disruption. Researchers found AirDrop bugs that could crash Apple’s sharing service. That service supports AirDrop and other continuity features.

On Samsung Quick Share, researchers found protocol weaknesses that could let an attacker manipulate connection behavior before full authentication. Another issue could allow certain control messages to be injected during an active transfer.

The Google Quick Share for Windows bug is more serious on paper. Researchers described it as a heap use-after-free issue and said Google awarded a bug bounty for it. The paper says this type of bug could potentially be developed into a full remote code-execution exploit.

Google told CyberGuy it has addressed the Windows issue. "We've patched the flaw identified for Quick Share for Windows. As a best security practice, users should always ensure they apply the latest security updates available for their device," a Google spokesperson said.
For most phone owners, the daily takeaway is clear. Nearby sharing is useful, but you should avoid leaving your device open to everyone when you do not need it.
Who faces the biggest AirDrop and Quick Share risk

You should be extra careful with AirDrop or Quick Share when you are around a lot of strangers. That includes airports, trains, hotels and large events. These are places where a nearby attacker could sit close enough to reach many devices at once.

The risk goes up when your phone is set to receive from everyone. On iPhone, Apple says the "Everyone for 10 Minutes" setting reverts after 10 minutes if you are signed in to your Apple Account. If you are not signed in, it reverts to Receiving Off. That time limit helps. Even so, you should treat "Everyone" as a temporary setting. Turn it on only when you need it.
Ways to stay safe from AirDrop and Quick Share risks

The good news is that a few quick settings checks can make your phone much harder for nearby strangers to reach. You can also review these iPhone and Android security settings for more ways to lock down your device.
A few quick settings checks can help keep your iPhone or Samsung phone from being visible to strangers nearby. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Start with regular software updates. The researchers responsibly disclosed the findings, and fixes are underway across vendors. Install iOS, iPadOS, macOS, Android, Samsung updates, Google Play system updates and Quick Share for Windows updates as soon as they become available. Also check the apps or utilities tied to sharing on your computer. Quick Share for Windows was part of this research, so remember the PC side if you use Android-to-Windows transfers.
On iPhone, keep AirDrop limited unless you are actively using it. The safest everyday choice is Receiving Off or Contacts Only.

To check AirDrop from Control Center on most newer iPhones, wake up your iPhone and unlock it. Look at the top-right corner of the screen where you see the battery icon. Place your finger near that corner and swipe down toward the middle of the screen. If Notification Center opens instead, try again from farther to the right.Next, look for the box in the top-left area with the Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and airplane icons. Touch and hold that box until it expands.Then tap AirDrop. Choose Receiving Off if you do not want anyone nearby to send you files. Choose Contacts Only if you only want people saved in your contacts to reach you.You can also use the Settings app. Tap Settings, then General, then AirDrop. From there, choose Receiving Off, Contacts Only or Everyone for 10 Minutes.Use Everyone for 10 Minutes only when you are expecting a file from someone nearby. After that, go back to AirDrop and switch it to Contacts Only or Receiving Off.

To check AirDrop from Control Center on most newer iPhones, wake up your iPhone and unlock it. Look at the top-right corner of the screen where you see the battery icon. Place your finger near that corner and swipe down toward the middle of the screen. If Notification Center opens instead, try again from farther to the right.
Next, look for the box in the top-left area with the Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and airplane icons. Touch and hold that box until it expands.
Then tap AirDrop. Choose Receiving Off if you do not want anyone nearby to send you files. Choose Contacts Only if you only want people saved in your contacts to reach you.
You can also use the Settings app. Tap Settings, then General, then AirDrop. From there, choose Receiving Off, Contacts Only or Everyone for 10 Minutes.
Use Everyone for 10 Minutes only when you are expecting a file from someone nearby. After that, go back to AirDrop and switch it to Contacts Only or Receiving Off.
On a Samsung phone, Quick Share controls who can see your device and send you files nearby. The safest everyday choice is No one or Contacts only.
GOOGLE TURNS OLD PHONES INTO CLOUD SERVERS

To check it from the Quick panel, wake up your phone and unlock it. Place two fingers at the very top-right area of the screen and swipe down. This opens the full Quick panel. If that feels tricky, swipe down once from the top of the screen, then swipe down again to see more buttons.Look for the Quick Share button. If you do not see it, swipe left across the Quick panel to see more buttons. Tap Quick Share.A menu should appear that says Who can share with you. Choose No one if you do not want nearby people to find your phone. Choose Contacts only if you only want saved contacts to share with you. Avoid Everyone or Anyone nearby unless you are expecting a file from someone you trust.You can also use the Settings app. Tap Settings, then tap the search bar at the top. Type Quick Share. Tap Quick Share, then tap Who can share with you. Choose No one or Contacts only.Use Everyone or Anyone nearby only when you are actively receiving a file. After that, go back into Quick Share and switch it to No one or Contacts only.

To check it from the Quick panel, wake up your phone and unlock it. Place two fingers at the very top-right area of the screen and swipe down. This opens the full Quick panel. If that feels tricky, swipe down once from the top of the screen, then swipe down again to see more buttons.
Look for the Quick Share button. If you do not see it, swipe left across the Quick panel to see more buttons. Tap Quick Share.

A menu should appear that says Who can share with you. Choose No one if you do not want nearby people to find your phone. Choose Contacts only if you only want saved contacts to share with you. Avoid Everyone or Anyone nearby unless you are expecting a file from someone you trust.
You can also use the Settings app. Tap Settings, then tap the search bar at the top. Type Quick Share. Tap Quick Share, then tap Who can share with you. Choose No one or Contacts only.
Use Everyone or Anyone nearby only when you are actively receiving a file. After that, go back into Quick Share and switch it to No one or Contacts only.

A file request from a stranger should be a red flag. Even if the file name looks harmless, decline it. Attackers often rely on curiosity. They may use a funny photo name or something that looks like it came from a nearby event. If you did not ask for the file, decline the request.

If you are traveling or sitting in a packed public place, turn receiving off. This is especially helpful at airports, train stations and large events. You can still turn AirDrop or Quick Share back on when you actually need it. That small habit gives you more control over when your phone is visible.

If you use AirDrop or Quick Share to send personal files, slow down before you tap send. Check the recipient name carefully. When possible, confirm the device in person before sharing. Be extra careful with photos, tax documents, travel confirmations, medical forms, school paperwork or anything that includes your address, phone number or financial details. Avoid sending private files to devices with generic names like "iPhone," "Galaxy" or "Laptop." For sensitive documents, use a trusted cloud storage or file-sharing service where you can confirm the recipient, manage access and add password protection when available.

Nearby sharing often relies on Bluetooth and Wi-Fi to discover and transfer between devices. You do not need to turn both off all day. However, it is smart to disable sharing features when you are done. Also, skip random public Wi-Fi networks just because they look familiar. Your phone can do a lot in the background. Give it fewer chances to talk to strangers.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious files if you accidentally accept something you should not have. This is especially important on computers, since Quick Share for Windows was part of the research. Keep your security software updated and scan any file that looks suspicious before opening it. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

AirDrop and Quick Share are useful, and most of us will keep using them. I know I will. But this research is a good reminder that nearby sharing should not stay wide open by default. The issue comes down to convenience. Phone makers made file sharing feel effortless. That is great when you are sending vacation photos to family or moving a file to your laptop. It feels different when the same feature is listening in a packed airport, coffee shop or hotel lobby. What stands out to me is the range. A bad actor may only need to be close by. So, my advice is straightforward. Update your devices. Keep AirDrop and Quick Share limited to people you trust. Turn off receiving when you are in a crowd. And never accept a file request you were not expecting.
Limiting AirDrop and Quick Share to trusted contacts can reduce the chances of unwanted file requests or risky transfers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

title: Trump administration has lost or abandoned hundreds of lawsuits against anti-ICE protesters, migrants: report
summary: A report said the Trump administration lost or abandoned hundreds of cases charging anti-ICE protesters and migrants with assaulting agents.
story: Former Acting DHS Secretary Chad Wolf discusses the White House's new guidance allowing I.C.E. agents to resume traffic stops if at least one agent is wearing a body camera following recent fatal shootings on 'America Reports.'
The Trump administration has lost or abandoned hundreds of cases in which it accused anti-ICE protesters and migrants of assaulting federal immigration agents, a report said.

An analysis from The New York Times showed that of the 558 people charged, 191 cases were dismissed, and 22 people were acquitted. Only four were convicted after trial, while 246 pleaded guilty and another 95 cases are pending.

The newspaper reported the Justice Department typically has a record of more than 90% of defendants pleading guilty or being convicted at trial. The Trump administration’s strategy in court has been leaning on 18 U.S.C. 111, a statute that makes it a federal crime to assault or forcibly impede a government officer and carries punishments ranging from a fine to 20 years in prison, it added.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and the Justice Department for comment.
NEW YORK TIMES TORCHED FOR 'FALSE' REPORTING ON ICE INVESTIGATIONS, OUTLET FIRES BACK

Federal agents are seen walking in uniform. A report from The New York Times said the Trump administration has lost or abandoned hundreds of cases in which it accused anti-ICE protesters and migrants of assaulting federal immigration agents. (John Moore/Getty Images)

DHS spokeswoman Lauren Bis told The New York Times that "it should come as no surprise that there’s an increase in criminal referrals under 18 U.S.C. 111 as there’s been a massive increase in violence and threats against federal law enforcement."

"Federal prosecutors are correct to prioritize these prosecutions and hold individuals accountable to the fullest extent of the law," added Justice Department spokesman Wyn Hornbuckle, describing how prosecutors, at times, reduced or dropped charges based on "mitigating factors identified in a case."
The New York Times cited another Justice Department official as saying that prosecutors in some of the cases dropped charges when the defendants were deported from the United States.
The newspaper said it based its analysis on court filings, hearing transcripts, videos of encounters and interviews with witnesses and federal officials.
ICE RESUMES NATIONWIDE TRAFFIC STOPS UNDER NEW POLICY REQUIRING BODY CAMERAS

A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent during a multi-agency targeted enforcement operation in Chicago, Illinois on Sunday, Jan. 26, 2025. (Christopher Dilts/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

It reported that in dozens of the cases that were lost or abandoned, court records and video showed that federal agents initiated physical struggles, such as shoving, tackling and pepper spraying defendants. Other defendants were able to successfully argue that the assaults they were accused of committing against the federal agents were acts of self-defense, the newspaper added.
Two of the judges overseeing the cases discovered agents purposely destroyed evidence, including demanding that a defendant delete images from their cellphone, according to The New York Times.

Officers also charged more than two dozen people who allegedly filmed or followed agents, sometimes honking car horns or shouting phrases like, "La migra is coming!," despite no allegations of physical contact with agents, the newspaper reported.

In one case, a judge dismissed assault charges against an immigrant after ruling that the agent involved was cut by glass from a car window that the agent had smashed, and in 65 instances, prosecutors abandoned or dropped charges before deadlines to present evidence to a grand jury or judge, the New York Times also said.
Anti-I.C.E. protesters face off with federal agents outside the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement building on Oct. 18, 2025, in Portland, Oregon. (Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The report did note one occasion when federal immigration officers were seriously hurt by protesters and migrants, including the dragging of an officer who had his arm inside a car window.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: ‘Hero' mom dies after using last strength to save 4-year-old son from Florida river
summary: Nicole Grayson, 43, jumped into the St. Johns River at Ed Stone Park to save her 4-year-old son, using all her strength to keep him above water.
story: ICE officer Gregory Simmonds describes the heroic moment he rescued a 6-year-old from drowning in a Florida pool on May 16, as captured by surveillance video. Simmonds jumped in fully clothed, pulled the unconscious child out and performed CPR to save the child's life. He also addresses current criticisms facing the agency.

A Florida "hero" mom died after using all her strength to keep her 4-year-old son above water when he fell into the St. Johns River, allowing rescuers to pull the boy to safety, authorities and her family said.
Nicole Grayson, 43, jumped into the river after her young son fell into the water at Ed Stone Park, west of DeLand, around 4 p.m. Saturday, according to the Volusia Sheriff’s Office.

Investigators said the child had been playing with an unidentified object near a wooden fence along the river’s edge when he dropped it over the barrier. The boy fell into the river while attempting to retrieve it.
OFF-DUTY ICE OFFICER RELIES ON 'SIXTH SENSE' TO SAVE DROWNING CHILD BEFORE DELIVERING MESSAGE TO CRITICS
Grayson immediately went in after him.
Nicole Grayson drowned after rescuing her 4-year-old son from the St. Johns River in Central Florida. (GoFundMe)

"My guess is he was trying to get it. He slipped in the water, deep, he slipped away in the water," Grayson’s oldest son, Dafino Devega, told FOX 35. "And then my mom, I guess she panicked, and she went in the water and tried to save him."
CROCODILE ATTACK HORROR UNFOLDS AS COUPLE TRIES TO SAVE VICTIM: ‘WE FELT SO HELPLESS’
As Grayson struggled to keep her son above the surface, a witness at the park flagged down a passing boater, who threw two life preservers toward the mother and child, the sheriff’s office said.
Grayson eventually became submerged while continuing to hold her son above the water.
A frantic 911 caller told dispatchers that rescuers had managed to reach the child but were still struggling to recover his mother.
FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT
"Hey 911, can you come to Ed Stone Park?" the caller said in audio obtained by FOX 35. "We have a mother that’s drowned, and we got the baby, but we can’t get the mama."

A memorial of daisies is placed near a fence where Volusia sheriff's deputies said a 4-year-old fell over into the St. Johns River on July 18. The child's mother drowned after she jumped in to save her son, according to deputies. (Patricio G. Balona / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

The boater maneuvered close enough to pull the 4-year-old aboard. The boy was unharmed, according to authorities.
Witness Jon Reaka said Grayson appeared to expend all her energy ensuring her son survived.
"She spent all her energy trying to get her kid up over the edge," Reaka told FOX 35.
Reaka jumped over a railing and onto the boat, where he helped pull Grayson from the river. She was unresponsive when she was brought aboard.

"I jumped over the rail, jumped onto the boat and pulled the lady up onto the boat and, you know, we started CPR — I started CPR and mouth-to-mouth immediately," Reaka said.
Emergency medical personnel took over lifesaving measures after arriving at the park. Grayson was rushed to a hospital, where efforts to revive her continued for several hours.
She died in the intensive care unit around 10 p.m. Saturday, the sheriff’s office said.

"I tried everything I could do to save her," Reaka told FOX 35. "You know, I feel horrible. I mean, it’s so sad what happened."
Grayson was a mother of six whose final act reflected the fiercely protective way she had lived, her family said.
"That’s the type of mom that she was; she was a hero," Devega said.
"My mom, she was a strong woman," he added. "She would do anything to keep her kids safe."

"Sheriff Chitwood and the entire Volusia Sheriff's Office send sincere thanks all who jumped in to help with the rescue, and deepest condolences to Ms. Grayson's family and friends for their loss of a mother who gave her life to save her son," the department said in a statement.

Chitwood said Grayson would be remembered as a hero, "not just because of her final heroic act, but because she was a mom who would do anything for her kids."

title: Woman's remains identified by DNA in Virginia, exposing second alleged murder linked to same 4 suspects
summary: DNA analysis identified Helen Marie Pullen Banks months after her remains were found, linking her death to four suspects in a second Virginia murder.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The four suspects accused of killing a Virginia teenager are now facing charges in a second homicide after investigators identified a woman whose remains remained a mystery for more than three months, revealing what authorities say were two connected, premeditated killings.

Helen Marie Pullen Banks, 56, of Culpeper, was identified through "extensive and complex DNA analysis" completed July 7, after her remains were discovered March 27 on private property in Caroline County, according to the sheriff's office.

Authorities announced this month that Rashad Antonio Mayfield, 21, Devonti Gregory Pettaway, 19, Jaden Lamont Phillips, 20, and Kennady Jade Lambert, 18, have each been charged with first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder and use of a firearm in the commission of murder in Banks' death.
WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT

Authorities say Kennady Jade Lambert, Devonti Gregory Pettaway, Jaden Lamont Phillips and Rashad Antonio Mayfield are charged in the murders of Helen Marie Pullen Banks and Jayden McComber. (Google Maps/Caroline County Sheriff's Office, VA)
All four suspects were already being held without bond after being charged with murder in the death of 18-year-old Jayden McComber.
Investigators say they suspected early in the case that the two homicide investigations were linked.

McComber disappeared the same day Banks' remains were discovered. His vehicle was recovered the following day in Virginia Beach with assistance from the Virginia Beach Police Department, according to the sheriff's office.
TEENS SUSPECTED OF MURDERING CONGRESSIONAL INTERN LINKED BY DNA ON SHELL CASINGS, PROSECUTORS SAY
Jayden McComber was 18 years old when he was killed in March 2026, according to investigators. (Virginia State Police)
Authorities said the vehicle was thoroughly processed and produced "valuable investigative leads" that helped investigators locate McComber's remains and identify the suspects.
McComber's body was found March 31 in a pond near the Caroline County line.

During an April 2 search of a Henrico County residence believed to be associated with Mayfield, investigators recovered personal belongings thought to have been in McComber's possession when he disappeared, authorities said.

Mayfield was arrested on charges during a traffic stop conducted while investigators were searching the residence. Authorities said a handgun was seized from his possession, though they have not disclosed whether the firearm has been linked to either homicide.

Pettaway, Phillips and Lambert were arrested during a simultaneous operation at an apartment on Kenway Avenue in Henrico. Caroline County investigators were assisted in the arrests by the U.S. Marshals Service Capital Area Regional Fugitive Task Force.

Following the arrests, Sheriff Scott Moser described the case as a "complex and difficult investigation" and praised the "relentless work" that led authorities to the four suspects.
The sheriff's office said ballistic testing performed with assistance from the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives later produced forensic evidence linking the two murders.

Investigators say both Banks and McComber knew at least one of the suspects before they were killed. However, authorities said they have uncovered no evidence that either victim had a conflict or dispute with the suspects over what investigators described as "premeditated and deliberate acts."
Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive or said whether Banks and McComber knew one another.
When Banks' remains were first discovered, the property owner who found them was "understandably shaken" and did not approach the body before calling 911, according to the sheriff's office.

"This is a deeply disturbing case," Moser said at the time. "The scene our deputies and investigators encountered was difficult, but they remained focused and professional from the moment they arrived."
Helen Marie Pullen Banks' identity remained unknown for more than three months before investigators identified her through DNA analysis. (Found and Sons Funeral Chapels & Cremation Service)

The sheriff's office later alleged that those responsible had taken "sick and deliberate" measures to conceal Banks' identity, calling it one of the more disturbing cases investigators had encountered. Authorities have not publicly detailed those alleged measures.
Banks' identity was formally confirmed July 7, and investigators met with her family that evening to notify them.

"This case reflects the relentless commitment of our investigators to pursue the truth," Moser said after announcing the identification. "While no announcement can ease the pain of this loss, we hope today's identification of Helen Marie Pullen Banks provides at least some measure of answers for her loved ones."

The investigation has also involved the Caroline County Commonwealth's Attorney's Office, FBI and ATF. Authorities said they are not searching for any additional suspects, though the case remains active.
The sheriff's office said Banks' family was notified of her identification on July 7 after DNA testing confirmed her identity.

Banks was born in Charlottesville and lived in Rixeyville, according to her obituary. She is survived by five children, her mother, two siblings, 10 grandchildren, one great-grandchild and a large extended family.
Helen Marie Pullen Banks, 56, was identified through DNA testing after her remains were discovered in Caroline County. (GoFundMe)

"Helen was so much more than the circumstances surrounding her passing," her family wrote in a GoFundMe established to help cover memorial expenses. "She was a daughter, a sister, a mother, a grandmother, and a great-grandmother."
McComber's family also remembered the 18-year-old in a GoFundMe created after his death, describing the week-long search for him as "a nightmare no family should ever have to live through."

"Jayden was so deeply loved," his family wrote. "He had the biggest heart and made sure the people around him knew it. He never missed a chance to say 'I love you,' and those words mean everything to us now."
The investigation remains active, though authorities say they are not seeking additional suspects.

title: Alleged 'mime' stalker stripped to underwear, covered himself in cooking oil: officials
summary: Massachusetts man Hernan Villagran Lux allegedly stripped to his underwear and slathered cooking oil on his body near female park workers before collapsing in court.
story: Hernan Villagran Lux, 29, was arrested by Massachusetts State Police on Sunday evening and appeared to faint on the stand in court this week. (Boston 25)
Not all mimes stay silent. One is now accused of terrorizing women.

A Massachusetts man known for roaming in a black-and-white mime costume is accused of frightening women for months at a popular state park, where prosecutors say he allegedly stripped to his underwear, slathered himself in cooking oil and worked out near female employees before later collapsing in court as the allegations were read aloud.

Hernan Villagran Lux, 29, of Framingham, is facing criminal harassment charges after three female state Department of Conservation and Recreation (DCR) employees had up to over 50 encounters over the past two months at a Natick state park near Boston.

Prosecutors said all three women knew Lux by name and appearance, and one reported more than 50 encounters that authorities said escalated over time, eventually leaving employees afraid to work around him.
FLORIDA MAN WHO ALLEGEDLY LURED WOMEN WITH DATING APP COULD HAVE MORE VICTIMS: AUTHORITIES
Appearing in court earlier this week, alleged "mime" stalker Hernan Villagran Lux, 29, fainted on the stand as his charges were read. (Boston 25 News)

The allegations have also sparked warnings on social media, where people across several Massachusetts communities said they recognized the suspect and claimed he had approached or followed women on a nearby rail trail.

Authorities arrested Lux Sunday night on the Cochituate Rail Trail, after multiple women and park workers alleged he repeatedly approached them, stared at them and refused to leave despite repeated requests, according to Boston 25 News.

"The women report an extensive number of contacts with the defendant involving him staring at them, smiling in what they describe as 'a really unnerving and frankly terrifying manner,'" Framingham District Court Supervisor Andrew Mange said during Monday's court hearing.
MAN ACCUSED OF REPEATEDLY TRESPASSING AT CIA HEADQUARTERS IN VIRGINIA
A sign marks the entrance to Cochituate State Park in Natick, Mass., where a man is accused of repeatedly harassing female park employees over several months. (Boston 25 News)

Mange said the encounters became increasingly bold. In one incident, prosecutors allege Lux "stripped down to his underwear, slathered cooking oil all over his body and began working out right by their staff area."
The women also reported that Lux repeatedly refused to leave the park after being asked to do so, according to the station.
Prosecutors also alleged Lux complimented one employee's appearance, commented on her lips and refused to leave as she and coworkers abandoned their work area because they felt unsafe.
Boston 25 reported that numerous people posted on social media saying they had spotted a man matching Lux's distinctive mime-like appearance throughout Framingham, Natick and Wayland.
Several women also claimed a man fitting the same description approached and followed them on the Cochituate Rail Trail.

Hernan Villagran Lux appears in Framingham District Court in Framingham, Mass., on criminal harassment charges stemming from allegations involving female employees at a state park outside Boston. (Boston 25 News)
"I spotted him, he looked kind of odd but I thought he was just dressed in a costume," neighbor Nancy Dlott told Boston 25. "It's kind of upsetting, especially if you're walking alone," she added.
"I just don't understand what goes through someone's head to do that," Christopher Labella told the station. "I hope this guy gets the help that he needs."

As prosecutors continued reading the allegations in court Monday, Lux fainted and was treated before proceedings resumed, according to Boston 25.
When court resumed later in the afternoon, the judge ordered Lux to undergo a mental health evaluation at Bridgewater State Hospital.

title: California toddler bitten by rattlesnake hiding beneath Amazon package amid active snake season
summary: A 3-year-old girl was bitten by a rattlesnake hiding beneath an Amazon package outside her California home and spent two days receiving antivenom.
story: Jesse Watters reports on a significant increase in snake bites across the United States this summer, noting that California has already exceeded its yearly quota for fatal bites. Watters details the severe injuries sustained by Chris, who required 36 vials of antivenom after a Western rattlesnake bite, and a 2-year-old girl in Colorado who was airlifted to the hospital following a rattlesnake attack.

A Southern California family is urging people to stay alert after their 3-year-old daughter was bitten by a rattlesnake hiding beneath an Amazon package outside their home, the latest in a string of snakebite incidents during an unusually active season across the state.
The frightening encounter comes weeks after a hiker was airlifted from a remote Ventura County trail following a rattlesnake bite.

Earlier this year, Ventura County firefighters told Fox News Digital they had responded to seven rattlesnake bites in roughly a month, and officials attributed the increase to warmer weather that has driven snakes out earlier than usual.

Manuel Barajas said his daughter, Addy, ran outside after her mother told her an Amazon package had been delivered and tossed over the family's front gate. As the 3-year-old reached for the padded envelope, a Southern Pacific rattlesnake concealed beneath it bit her on the left hand.
TOURIST DIES AT LUXURY RESORT AFTER COBRA FROM SNAKE SHOW CLIMBS UP PANTS, BITES HIM: POLICE

A Southern Pacific rattlesnake is held by a wrangler in Landers, Calif. A 3-year-old California girl was recently bitten by the species after it hid beneath an Amazon package outside her home. (Gina Ferazzi/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images, File)

Her mother rushed Addy to a nearby grocery store parking lot, where paramedics met the family before transporting her to a hospital. She was later transferred to a pediatric intensive care unit, where she spent two days receiving additional doses of antivenom.

Wildlife experts say an unusually warm spring has fueled increased rattlesnake activity across California this year, contributing to a rise in snakebite incidents and three reported snakebite deaths statewide.

The latest incident follows several other serious encounters this year. In May, a woman hiking in Ventura County was airlifted to a hospital after being bitten by a rattlesnake on a remote trail. A Thousand Oaks woman also died in March after being bitten while hiking at Wildwood Regional Park.
TICK BITE ER VISITS HIT HIGHEST SEASONAL LEVEL IN YEARS AS DOCTORS WARN OF DISEASE SURGE
The snake was underneath a padded Amazon package when it lunged at the 3-year-old child. (Lindsey Nicholson/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images, File)
Health officials say anyone bitten by a rattlesnake should seek emergency medical care immediately, remain as still as possible and avoid attempting home remedies that can worsen the injury.

Barajas told Nexstar's KTLA he hopes sharing his family's experience will encourage others to stay vigilant around their homes and know which hospitals are equipped to treat pediatric snakebite emergencies.
Experts say California has seen increased rattlesnake activity this year. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images, File)

"She’s doing great now. She’s, I want to say, about 70% recovered," Barajas said. "She’s still bruised on her left hand where she was bitten. Her spirits are high, her demeanor is great, but she keeps asking why she was bitten by a snake."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
A GoFundMe campaign has been launched to help the family cover Addy's medical expenses and lost income while she continues to recover.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Army veteran faces arson charge after attack outside NYC federal building: 'Came armed with bad intentions'
summary: Videos show fire and bright orange flames outside 26 Federal Plaza as Andrew Arrabaca allegedly fired an airsoft rifle at the federal building.
story: Video shows suspect Andrew Arrabaca allegedly pouring gasoline and setting a fire outside Manhattan’s 16 Federal Plaza, home to New York City’s immigrant court and ICE offices.

The U.S. Army veteran accused of setting a fire outside a New York City federal building that houses an immigration court and other government agencies, including the FBI, and firing a pellet gun, will face an arson charge related to the Monday attack, which he had been planning for months, federal prosecutors said.
Andrew Arrabaca, 43, appeared in a Manhattan federal court Tuesday for his alleged actions outside 26 Federal Plaza that injured three people before he was subdued.
He did not enter a plea.
U.S. Magistrate Judge Robyn F. Tarnofsky, noted that the attack could have ended tragically.

"The crime you’re charged with is troubling," said Tarnofsky, who immediately conducted a bail hearing and ordered Arrabaca to be released to a mental health facility. The judge said the alleged attack was "planned over time" and "wasn't something that was done on a Sunday."
FBI ARRESTS PROTESTER WHO THREATENED TO KILL ICE OFFICER'S FAMILY AT NJ DETENTION CENTER PROTEST, BLANCHE SAYS
Authorities apprehended a suspect outside a federal building in New York City on Monday. (FNTV)

Arrabaca, who served as a mechanic on Patriot missile systems in the Army, harbored anti-ICE and anti-government views, James Barnacle, assistant director in charge of the FBI's New York Field Office, said Monday.
"He is an anti-American, anti-government extremist," Barnacle told reporters at the scene.
Voter records show he has registered as a Democrat and was a member of the left-wing Working Families party.
Andrew Arrabaca, 43, is charged with arson for allegedly setting a fire outside 26 Federal Plaza in New York City on Monday.  (Justice Department)

Arrabaca "came armed with bad intentions" and was found with a range of weapons, including a pellet gun, knives, a hammer, and a machete. Authorities said the upstate New York resident arrived at the federal building sometime around 8:30 a.m. and lit a large firework before pouring a liquid that ignited a fire.
Videos and images from the scene showed a fire with a plume of smoke and bright orange flames near a building entrance, as well as law enforcement officers restraining the suspect.
VIDEO SHOWS MOMENT CHICAGO MAN ALLEGEDLY USED SUV AS WEAPON AGAINST ICE AGENT, PROSECUTORS SAY

In addition to allegedly setting the fire, Arrabaca also fired five to seven pellets from an airsoft rifle toward the building, Barnacle said. He was arrested by federal officials a short time later and has been in custody since.

He made several anti-government and anti-ICE statements during the incident and said "he was okay if he hurt or killed people going in and out of the building, whether they were federal employees or civilians," the FBI said.
Upon his arrest, authorities said they found Arrabaca with two axes, a hammer, a machete and three knives.

Prosecutors said he had arrived pulling a four-wheeled utility wagon bearing a sign that read "ICE Off Our Streets," which also contained BB and pellet rifles, fireworks and a consumer firework labeled "Nuclear Warhead." Arrabaca was also wearing a helmet bearing several phrases, including "Kill yourself," according to the criminal complaint
Federal prosecutors said he had been planning the attack since January, when he began buying supplies and visiting sites around New York.

Arrabaca allegedly told law enforcement that he went to several other sites around the city bringing materials and considered attacking them. After months, he decided to attack the federal building near the courthouse.
A federal officer investigates the scene after an incendiary device went off outside 26 Federal Plaza in Lower Manhattan early on Monday in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
On Sunday, he made his way to Lower Manhattan with the weapons and other items used during the attack, prosecutors allege. He spent the night in a park and arrived at the building on Monday morning.
He told law enforcement he targeted a specific entrance because it was busy and employees were heading to work and members of the public were heading inside.
Arrabaca admitted that he was aware people could be hurt and was willing to accept the risk, said prosecutors, who described his actions as "calculated." He was also aware he could die.

Surveillance images included in the complaint show people standing just feet from the entrance when Arrabaca allegedly ignited the flammable liquid, while prosecutors say at least one victim suffered a gash to the back of the head after being struck by debris from the fire or explosion.

Defense lawyer Jennifer Brown said Arrabaca has mental health issues, and asked that he be placed in a Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) mental health hospital for evaluation and treatment. Prosecutors noted that Arrabaca does not have a stable residence or employment and was living out of a car before the attack.

"The mental health issues that are quite likely the cause of the behavior, I seriously considered the alternatives proposed by Ms. Brown, but I had to reject them because I don’t think it’s sufficiently clear you would comply with treatment," Tarnofsky told Arrabaca.
Andrew Arrabaca, 43, allegedly fire several rounds from a pellet gun after setting the fire.  (Justice Department)

The federal building in Lower Manhattan has been the scene of protests against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency charged with enforcing the nation's immigration laws amid the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration.

One of two people hurt during Monday's incident was an immigrant who appeared at the building for a hearing, the FBI said.
A preliminary hearing is scheduled for Aug. 4. He faces a mandatory minimum of seven years in prison.
Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price and Michael Ruiz contributed to this report.

title: Singer D4vd shows no emotion as detective recounts gruesome discovery of teen's dismembered remains: report
summary: Gruesome testimony revealed maggots and flies in the Tesla trunk where prosecutors say D4vd left 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez's remains.
story: Rising recording artist David Burke, known as D4vd, is accused of murdering and dismembering a 14-year-old girl just two days before his first album dropped.

The California singer accused of grooming a 14-year-old girl only to murder her when she threatened to expose him and then dismembering her remains with a chainsaw appeared in front of a Los Angeles judge Tuesday for the first day of a preliminary hearing expected to clear the way for the case to go to trial.

David Burke, who performs under the name "D4vd," is accused of killing a teen girl named Celeste Rivas Hernandez, whose unrecognizable remains prosecutors say were found chopped up and decomposing in the trunk of his Tesla, abandoned 400 feet up the street from his home in Hollywood Hills.
Two of her fingers, which contained identifying tattoos, were never recovered.
Burke faces charges of murder, child sex abuse and unlawful mutilation of human remains.
RISING SINGER DISMEMBERED TEEN WHO THREATENED TO EXPOSE HIM IN KIDDIE POOL WITH CHAINSAW: DA
Singer D4vd was arrested in Los Angeles in the murder of a 14-year-old girl found in a Tesla trunk, police say. (Timothy Norris/Getty Images for Coachella)

Prior to the hearing, which is expected to take about three to five days, Celeste's parents, Jesus Rivas and Mercedes Martinez, were spotted entering the Los Angeles County District Attorney's Office.
There were no cameras allowed in the courtroom Tuesday as prosecutors displayed gruesome images and shared brutal details with the court.

A Los Angeles homicide detective took the stand to discuss the grisly scene, with Celeste's parents opting to remain in the gallery when given a chance to leave before his testimony, according to FOX 11 Los Angeles.

"There were maggots," LAPD Det. Joshua Byers testified, according to the California Post. "There were flies. I don't know how to describe the other liquid matter."
Martinez looked like she might faint as a supporter leaned over to help her, according to the FOX LA report. Burke, shackled to a chair, reportedly showed no visible reaction.

The parents of Celeste Rivas, Jesus Rivas and Mercedes Martinez, arrive to the Hall of Justice in Los Angeles, Tuesday, July 21, 2026. Their daughter's alleged killer, D4vd, is in a pretrial hearing for the murder case. (Jef Steinberg/Splash for Fox News Digital)
Prosecutors allege that Burke first met Celeste when she was 11 and began molesting her in November 2023, when she was 13 and he was 18.
Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters outside the courthouse that a decision on whether to seek the death penalty has not yet been made.

Prosecutors expect to call 10 witnesses, including members of the police department and coroner's office.

Burke and Celeste spent "a significant amount of time" together in 2024, when Burke allegedly flew the child to Las Vegas, London and Texas and introduced her to his family, prosecutors have alleged in court filings. In November of that year, however, they "broke up."

"[Text] messages reveal the victim's jealousy over defendant's relationships with other women, as defendant led her to believe they had a future together," prosecutors wrote. "She became extremely upset and threatened to disclose damaging information about her relationship with defendant to end his career and destroy his life."
SINGER D4VD PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO MURDER OF YOUNG GIRL ALLEGEDLY FOUND DISMEMBERED, DECOMPOSING IN HIS CAR

That was two days before his debut album dropped. Burke allegedly ordered Celeste an Uber and is accused of concocting a "plan to cover up the murder" that involved sending text messages to her phone asking where she was — allegedly after he'd already stabbed her to death.

title: Woman attacked by brown bear while hiking with friend and 3 dogs near Alaska state park
summary: A woman was injured after a brown bear attacked her on an overgrown trail area near Chugach State Park before rescuers safely evacuated her, police said.
story: A woman is recovering after a sudden brown bear encounter in Anchorage July 18, 2026, led officers to deploy a drone while firefighters evacuated her down a hillside. (Anchorage Police)
A woman was attacked by a brown bear Saturday while hiking with a friend and three dogs near a state park in Alaska, authorities said.
The woman sustained non-life-threatening injuries and is expected to recover, the Anchorage Police Department (APD) said Sunday.

The attack happened late afternoon near the Bear Valley residential neighborhood, adjacent to Chugach State Park in south Anchorage, the Alaska Department of Fish and Game (ADF&G) said in a separate statement on Monday.
TERRIFIED HIKERS FACE NIGHTMARE SURVIVAL SCENARIO AFTER HEART-POUNDING GRIZZLY BEAR ENCOUNTER
A brown bear moves through dense vegetation near Chugach State Park in Anchorage, Alaska, Saturday. (Anchorage Police Department)

Officials said the hikers were on an unofficial, user-made trail that climbs a steep hillside in a zigzag pattern. The area was heavily overgrown with dense vegetation, which created poor visibility and increased the risk of surprising wildlife, ADF&G said.
"The bear came out of the dense alders, made brief contact with one of the hikers, and left the scene," ADF&G said.

One of the victim's dogs was also off leash during the encounter and became separated from the group, according to the authorities. Another group of hikers later found the "uninjured dog and brought it back to safety, ultimately returning it to its home," ADF&G said.
HIDDEN DANGER AT POPULAR US NATIONAL PARK FORCES TRAIL CLOSURES AS BEAR SIGHTINGS CLIMB
Aerial police footage captures a brown bear navigating thick alders near Anchorage, Alaska, Saturday after a sudden encounter with hikers. (Anchorage Police Department)
According to wildlife officials, bears are known to cache and defend food sources this time of year and noted reports that at least one moose had recently been killed nearby.

"High winds and inclement weather conditions at the time of the encounter may have increased the chance that the bear was surprised by the hikers and their dogs, even if they were making noise," ADF&G said.
BEAR ATTACK IN YELLOWSTONE NATIONAL PARK LEAVES 2 HIKERS INJURED

"There are many private and public trails throughout Anchorage and the surrounding area that are overgrown at this time of year with tall grass and leafed out shrubs, which can greatly increase the chances of surprise encounters with wildlife."
A thermal drone camera pinpoints a brown bear on a steep hillside near Anchorage, Alaska, on Saturday. (Anchorage Police Department)
First responders from multiple agencies, including the Anchorage Fire Department, Alaska Wildlife Troopers and Alaska State Troopers, responded.
Upon arrival, police officers reportedly hiked up the trail to locate the injured adult.

Firefighters then carried the injured woman down the trail before transporting her to a hospital.

During the rescue, APD officers deployed a drone and located a brown bear nearby. Officers continued monitoring the bear throughout the rescue, allowing first responders to safely treat and evacuate the injured hiker.

title: Sharpton offers $50K for Nolan Wells case arrest with lawyer to release autopsy at NAACP
summary: Ben Crump plans to reveal independent autopsy findings in the Nolan Wells case at the NAACP National Convention as Al Sharpton offers a $50,000 reward.
story: The parents and attorneys of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, who was found dead after a 4th of July trip with friends, say they are launching an independent investigation.

Rev. Al Sharpton is offering a $50,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction in the death of Mississippi teenager Nolan Wells as attorney Ben Crump prepares to reveal preliminary findings Wednesday from an independent autopsy that could provide the first public medical insight into the 18-year-old's mysterious death.

Crump is expected to announce the findings during a news conference at the 117th NAACP National Convention in Chicago, where he will appear alongside Wells' parents, Christine and Elmore Wonsley. The family's legal team plans to release the first public findings from the independent examination.

The announcement comes days after the NAACP adopted a resolution urging local, state and federal authorities, including the U.S. Department of Justice, to conduct what it described as an in-depth and transparent investigation into Wells' death.
SEARCH CALLED OFF AFTER BODY MATCHING MISSING TEEN NOLAN WELLS FOUND OFF MISSISSIPPI COAST
Nolan Wells smiles on the field while playing wide receiver for Southwest Mississippi Community College. (Christine Wonsley/Facebook)

The footage pans across dozens of boats and people in the water before briefly focusing on an individual TMZ identified as Wells, though Fox News Digital has not independently verified the video's authenticity, when it was recorded or the identity of the person shown.

Wells disappeared July 4 after traveling by boat with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi's Gulf Coast, to celebrate Independence Day. Search crews spent two days looking for the teenager before a National Park Service ranger found his body near the island's northwestern tip on July 6. Authorities have not announced a cause or manner of death, and the investigation remains ongoing.
The official autopsy has not yet been released, making Wednesday's announcement the first independent medical findings expected to be shared publicly.

Rev. Al Sharpton speaks during a recent appearance. Sharpton has announced a $50,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction in the death of Mississippi teenager Nolan Wells. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)

title: Texas real estate agent suspected in nearly 100-stab cold case posted global vacations before arrest
summary: Surveillance video from 2012 showed a hooded figure entering Irasema Chavez's apartment the night before she was found stabbed roughly 100 times.
story: Mayra Velasquez, 42, has been charged with murder in the 2012 killing of 32-year-old Irasema Chavez. (KDFW-TV)
More than a decade after a Texas woman was found stabbed roughly 100 times in her apartment, a real estate agent is behind bars without bond, facing capital murder charges.
Mayra Velasquez, 42, was booked into the Tarrant County Corrections Center July 17 in the killing of Irasema Chavez, according to the Arlington Police Department and county jail records.

Chavez, 32, was found dead Jan. 20, 2012, inside her second-floor apartment in the 2700 block of South Collins Street. Investigators said there were no obvious signs of forced entry, raising the possibility that Chavez knew the person who killed her or willingly opened the door.
DNA CRACKS 40-YEAR COLD CASE MYSTERY WITH ARREST IN LIBRARY WORKER’S SAVAGE SLAYING: POLICE
Mayra Velasquez, 42, has been charged with murder in the 2012 killing of 32-year-old Irasema Chavez. (Tarrant County Jail)

Surveillance video obtained by KDFW-TV from the night before the grisly discovery showed a person wearing baggy clothing and a hoodie climbing the stairs to Chavez’s unit. The figure knocked, appeared to exchange words with someone at the door and was then allowed inside.
Police released the video in hopes the public could identify the visitor, but the shadowy image failed to produce the break detectives needed. The case eventually went cold.

title: FBI nabs alleged $547M Medicare fraud fugitive overseas, third capture from 'Most Wanted Fraudsters' list
summary: Khalid Ahmed Satary allegedly billed Medicare $547 million for unnecessary genetic tests on elderly patients before fleeing the country in 2022.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

FIRST ON FOX: The FBI has captured a fugitive accused of stealing more than half a billion dollars from Medicare and leading authorities on an international manhunt, marking the third arrest from the bureau's "Most Wanted Fraudsters" list.

Khalid Ahmed Satary, who was indicted in 2019 in the Southern District of Florida, was arrested overseas after spending nearly three years on the run, according to the FBI. Authorities said Satary violated the conditions of his pretrial release in 2022, prompting a federal arrest warrant.

"The arrest of Khalid Ahmed Satary and return to the U.S. is the third Most Wanted Fraudster capture from this FBI and our partners in just five weeks — continuing the historic run of success for this new initiative," FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital in a statement.
FBI CAPTURES $1.2B MEDICARE FRAUD FUGITIVE IN PHILIPPINES, SECOND ARREST FROM MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS LIST
Khalid Ahmed Satary was arrested overseas after spending nearly three years on the run, according to the FBI. (FBI)

Patel said Satary is accused of participating in a conspiracy that fraudulently billed Medicare for $547 million worth of expensive and medically unnecessary genetic tests between 2016 and 2019. According to the FBI, the scheme relied on deceptive marketing campaigns, illegal kickbacks and bribes to generate fraudulent Medicare claims.

"This defendant allegedly orchestrated a massive fraud scheme that preyed on thousands of elderly patients, deceiving them into undergoing expensive, medically unnecessary tests and fraudulently billing the government for more than half a billion dollars," acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "Thanks to the outstanding work of our partners at the FBI, this defendant was brought back from overseas to face justice in the United States. Our message to fraudsters is clear: If you steal from American taxpayers and exploit vulnerable patients, we will find and prosecute you, no matter where you are."
Patel said Satary "exploited a program dedicated to helping our most vulnerable and instead stole for himself."
Satary is accused of participating in a conspiracy that fraudulently billed Medicare for $547 million worth of expensive and medically unnecessary genetic tests between 2016 and 2019. (FBI)

The FBI said Satary was apprehended overseas through coordination with U.S. and international law enforcement partners and was expected to land in the United States Tuesday morning. He was scheduled to make his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday afternoon. The case is being handled by the FBI's Miami Field Office.
MINNESOTA MAN MARKS FBI'S FIRST ARREST FROM DOJ'S 'MOST WANTED FRAUDSTERS' LIST

"This defendant is alleged to have engaged in a massive fraud scheme that preyed on elderly patients, duped them into taking expensive and unnecessary genetic tests, and billed the United States more than half a billion dollars," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division said. "As today's arrest shows, there is no safe haven for fraudsters who seek to exploit vulnerable Americans or our Nation's critical health care programs."
Patel also linked Satary's arrest to the Trump administration's broader effort to combat fraud against taxpayers.
Satary's arrest marks the third capture since the FBI launched its Most Wanted Fraudsters list five weeks ago, Patel said. (FBI)

"This is just the latest example showing President Trump's and Vice President Vance's White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud will not be deterred in our mission to track down each and every fraudster who allegedly steals from American taxpayers," Patel said. "And it's yet another high-value target returned from overseas by this FBI — the 27th such transfer since June."

Satary's arrest marks the third capture since the FBI launched its Most Wanted Fraudsters list five weeks ago, an initiative aimed at locating and apprehending fugitives accused of large-scale financial crimes.
